groups.title: simplify dispatch: caller can observe a still-in-flight async Task write as "done"
groups.body:
Origin: reflect light from #2621
Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`/claude-tweaks:simplify`'s Step 2 dispatches the `code-simplifier:code-simplifier` subagent via the `Agent` tool, which is asynchronous — the dispatch call returns immediately with an `agentId`, and the caller is told "you know nothing about its results until [a] notification arrives." Step 2's own guidance ("Before committing the returned changes, the caller should diff them against its own change scope and revert anything outside it") assumes the caller can check `git status`/`git diff` once, right after dispatch, and see the agent's *final* state. During this review's Step 5 (record #2621), the caller (this flow run) checked `git status` shortly after dispatch, saw one out-of-scope file modified, reverted it (`git checkout --`), and moved on — only to find on a later, unrelated check that the agent had *continued writing* after that revert, producing a second, larger wave of out-of-scope edits (a `cmdNextTarget` refactor in `harness-health.js`) that required a second `git checkout --` pass to reach a clean tree. Because the Agent tool's async notification is the only reliable "the agent is truly done" signal, and the coordinating call cannot poll/sleep-loop for it, a caller that does the diff-and-revert check on its own initiative (rather than waiting for the completion notification) has no guarantee it is looking at final state.

## Deliverables

Clarify `skills/simplify/SKILL.md` Step 2's diff-and-revert guidance to state explicitly that the revert check must run only after the dispatch's completion notification has been received (not on an ad hoc `git status` poll), or provide an explicit "wait for this dispatch" primitive callers can use without violating the "never end this turn waiting" constraint documented elsewhere in this same plugin's dispatch guidance.

## Acceptance Criteria

`skills/simplify/SKILL.md`'s Step 2 names the completion-notification requirement (or an equivalent wait primitive) as a precondition for the diff-and-revert check, so a caller following the instructions as written cannot repeat this race.

groups.title: Add App Store rejection checklist for vibecoded apps
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
AI-built/vibecoded mobile apps commonly get rejected by Apple App Store review for a recurring cluster of well-known, documented reasons: Stripe checkout instead of in-app purchase, Google sign-in present but no Apple sign-in, no way for a user to delete their account, a broken or incomplete demo/reviewer login, broken iPad layout, screenshots that don't match the shipped app or show paid features without labeling them as paid, dead support/privacy links, "coming soon" placeholder screens, comment/UGC features with no report path, and a broken restore-purchases button. No existing claude-tweaks check walks a codebase through Apple App Store submission requirements specifically; the existing pre-scale and security work (#2622, #2624, #2625) covers backend scaling and data handling, not store-review compliance.

## Deliverables
1. Add an "App Store submission readiness" checklist — either as a new skill or as policy rows on an existing review skill (whichever integration point exists once this is built) — covering: Apple sign-in parity with any other social sign-in, in-app purchase vs. external payment links, account-deletion flow, demo/reviewer login completeness, iPad layout, screenshot accuracy including paid-feature labeling, live support/privacy links, no coming-soon placeholders, a moderation/report path for UGC comment features, and a working restore-purchases button.
2. Ship a copy-paste prompt, matching this pipeline's existing pattern for this class of check, that scans a mobile app's codebase/config for each of the ten gaps above.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Running the check against a sample mobile app codebase flags any of the ten gaps that are present.
2. Documentation distinguishes this store-review checklist's scope from the existing pre-launch/pre-scale hardening checks (#2622, #2624, #2625) so a reader doesn't confuse app-store compliance with backend scaling/security.
3. The check (and its copy-paste prompt) works standalone and as a step within `/claude-tweaks:review` or `/claude-tweaks:build`.
4. Each of the ten checklist items maps to a specific, checkable condition in a codebase or app config (e.g. "grep for a Stripe checkout SDK call alongside no `StoreKit`/`RevenueCat` import" for the payment-method item), not a vague prose reminder.

## Technical Approach
Add the checklist as a new prompt/heuristic in the same style as this pipeline's other copy-paste-prompt checks, choosing the integration point (new skill vs. rows on an existing review skill) based on whichever shape the existing review-skill surface supports by the time this is built. Each of the ten items becomes one checkable row: a description of the Apple-review failure mode, and a concrete signal to grep/inspect for in a mobile codebase (SDK imports, Info.plist/AndroidManifest entries, presence/absence of an account-deletion API call, screenshot metadata, etc.).

### Key Files
- Whichever file the App Store readiness checklist lands in (a new skill directory, or an existing review skill's policy file) — to be determined based on the review-skill surface's shape at build time
- A documentation note distinguishing this checklist's scope from #2622/#2624/#2625

## Gotchas
This is a mobile-specific (iOS App Store) checklist; it does not cover Google Play's parallel review criteria, which differ in several respects (e.g. Play doesn't mandate Apple/Google sign-in parity the same way). Scope this record to Apple App Store review only, and treat Play Store review as a separate future record if pursued. The exact integration point (new skill vs. existing skill's policy rows) can't be pinned until whatever review-skill surface exists at build time is inspected.

## Original request

Add App Store rejection checklist for vibecoded apps

Current State:
- AI-built/vibecoded apps commonly get rejected by Apple review for a recurring cluster of reasons: Stripe checkout instead of in-app purchase, Google sign-in present but no Apple sign-in, no way for a user to delete their account, a broken or incomplete demo/reviewer login, broken iPad layout, screenshots that don't match the shipped app or show paid features without labeling them as paid, dead support/privacy links, "coming soon" placeholder screens, comment/UGC features with no report path, and a broken restore-purchases button.
- No existing claude-tweaks check walks a codebase through Apple App Store submission requirements specifically; the existing pre-scale and security work (#2622, #2624, #2625) covers backend scaling and data handling, not store-review compliance.

Deliverables:
- Add an "App Store submission readiness" checklist (a skill or policy rows on an existing review skill) covering: Apple sign-in parity with any other social sign-in, in-app purchase vs. external payment links, account-deletion flow, demo/reviewer login completeness, iPad layout, screenshot accuracy including paid-feature labeling, live support/privacy links, no coming-soon placeholders, a moderation/report path for UGC comment features, and a working restore-purchases button.
- Ship a copy-paste prompt, matching the pipeline's existing pattern, that scans a mobile app's codebase/config for each gap.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Running the check against a sample app flags any of the gaps that are present.
- Docs distinguish this store-review checklist from the existing pre-launch/pre-scale hardening checks (#2622, #2624, #2625).
- Works standalone and as a step within /review or /build.

Source: https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dc_D90BBGG7/

groups.title: Add GDPR account-deletion vs. backup-retention check
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
Deleting a user from the production database on account deletion leaves their personal data intact in rolling database backups (e.g. a 30-day retention window), which can violate GDPR right-to-erasure. Rewriting, decrypting, and recompressing terabytes of backup data to scrub one user on every deletion request is operationally expensive and can overwhelm production systems. Cryptographic erasure — encrypting each user's sensitive data with a unique per-user key and destroying only that key on deletion — makes the backup copy unreadable without ever touching the backup itself. This project's pre-launch security hardening checklist (#2624, open, priority:medium) is being built for AI-built apps but currently has no check for this specific data-retention/right-to-erasure gap.

## Deliverables
1. Add a data-retention/right-to-erasure check — as a new row in the pre-launch security checklist being built under #2624, or as its own standalone policy row if #2624 lands first without this scope — that flags whether the app's backup/retention strategy leaves deleted users' data readable, and whether per-user field-level encryption is in place for data that lands in backups.
2. Document the cryptographic-erasure pattern (per-user key encryption + key destruction on deletion) as the recommended fix when a project keeps rolling backups containing user PII.
3. Ship a copy-paste prompt, matching this pipeline's existing pattern for this class of check, that walks a codebase through checking for this specific gap.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Running the check against a sample app flags whether a deleted user's data would remain readable in existing backups after an account-deletion flow runs.
2. The shipped documentation/policy content notes its relationship to the pre-launch security checklist (#2624) so the two records' scope doesn't duplicate — whichever lands first, the other references it rather than re-deriving the same check.
3. The check (and its copy-paste prompt) works standalone and as a step within `/claude-tweaks:review` or a security-review pass.
4. The documented recommended-fix pattern (cryptographic erasure) is described generically enough to apply across storage backends, not tied to one specific database or cloud vendor's backup product.

## Technical Approach
Coordinate scope with #2624: if #2624's checklist already has a data-retention section by the time this is built, extend it with this specific right-to-erasure-vs-backup-retention row; otherwise ship this as its own standalone policy/check entry that #2624 can later reference. Write the check as a prompt/heuristic (in the same style as this pipeline's other copy-paste-prompt checks) that inspects a codebase's backup/retention configuration and data-deletion code path for evidence of per-user field-level encryption versus plaintext PII landing in backups. Document the cryptographic-erasure pattern as the recommended remediation, generically (not vendor-specific).

### Key Files
- Whichever file(s) #2624's pre-launch security checklist lands in (to be determined once #2624 is shaped/built) — the natural home for this check if it lands first
- A new standalone policy/check file (if #2624 has not yet defined a home) documenting the GDPR account-deletion vs. backup-retention check and the cryptographic-erasure remediation pattern

## Gotchas
This record's scope is coupled to #2624's timing and final shape — the exact file(s) this check's row lands in can't be pinned until #2624 is itself shaped/built, since #2624 is the natural home. If #2624 ships without a data-retention section, this record's Deliverable 1 falls back to a standalone policy row instead, per the Technical Approach above. Whoever builds this should re-check #2624's current state (open/shaped/merged) before deciding which of the two paths applies.

## Original request

Add GDPR account-deletion vs. backup-retention check

Current State:
- Deleting a user from the production database on account deletion leaves their personal data intact in rolling database backups (e.g. a 30-day retention window), which can violate GDPR right-to-erasure.
- Rewriting, decrypting, and recompressing terabytes of backup data to scrub one user on every deletion request is operationally expensive and can overwhelm production systems.
- Cryptographic erasure — encrypting each user's sensitive data with a unique per-user key and destroying only that key on deletion — makes the backup copy unreadable without ever touching the backup itself.

Deliverables:
- Add a data-retention/right-to-erasure check to the existing pre-launch security checklist (issue #2624) or as its own policy row: does the app's backup/retention strategy leave deleted users' data readable, and is per-user field-level encryption in place for data that lands in backups?
- Document the cryptographic-erasure pattern as the recommended fix when a project keeps rolling backups containing user PII.
- Ship a copy-paste prompt, matching the pipeline's existing pattern, that walks a codebase through checking for this gap.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Running the check against a sample app flags whether a deleted user's data would remain readable in existing backups.
- Docs note the relationship to the pre-launch security checklist (#2624) so scope doesn't duplicate.
- Works standalone and as a step within /review or /security-review.

groups.title: review step3 dispatch: the SCRATCH path under the main-checkout run dir is unwritable for agents in a worktree-always session (empirical reproduction of closed #2245)
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`/claude-tweaks:review`'s Step 3 lens/refutation dispatch prompts (`plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md` line 72, `plugin/skills/review/step3-debate-and-refutation.md` lines 96 and 131) each hand every dispatched agent a line of the form `SCRATCH: {ctx-dir}/agent-scratch/{agent-id}`, citing `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule ("any probe script or fixture the agent creates to verify its own work goes there ... and is deleted before the status word"). `{ctx-dir}` is minted by `bin/build-review-context.js` under the pipeline run directory, which is anchored under the main checkout.

`_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule already documents one related failure mode, empirically confirmed on the earlier report #2245: when the scratch directory lies outside the agent's own worktree (an `EnterWorktree`-isolated dispatch whose `{ctx-dir}` resolves to the shared main checkout — "the case a review fan-out hits on every `worktree`-mode run"), a `Write`/`Edit` tool call is refused outright by the harness's worktree-pinning guard, but the documented workaround is to create/delete the scratch file via Bash instead (`mkdir -p` + a shell redirect/heredoc, then `rm`) — the guard is scoped to the file-editing tools, not to Bash.

This record (#2595) is the empirical reproduction of #2245's *further* concern under a `worktree-always: true` project: two refutation agents dispatched during a real `/claude-tweaks:flow #N` run (2026-09-18, plugin 6.126.0) both reported the guard refusing every write to their assigned `SCRATCH:` path, and fell back to ad hoc workarounds (inline `python -c` probes; one agent created and removed its own `/tmp` directory) rather than the Bash-mediated workaround `subagent-output-contract.md` already documents. Whether those agents simply weren't instructed to use the Bash-mediated approach (the `SCRATCH:` dispatch lines in `step3-lens-dispatch.md`/`step3-debate-and-refutation.md` don't explicitly repeat the "use Bash, not Write/Edit" instruction inline) or whether `worktree-always`'s guard additionally refuses Bash-mediated writes to the same path (a stricter regime than the narrower `EnterWorktree`-isolation case the existing Scratch rule text addresses) is not yet established — this needs to be determined as part of the fix, since it changes whether the existing documented workaround already suffices or whether a genuinely different scratch location is needed.

Regardless of mechanism, the consequences observed: nothing was lost, but the "delete your scratch before your status word" contract cannot be honoured, each agent spends turns discovering the refusal before working around it, and the post-fan-out scratch sweep (`step3-lens-dispatch.md`'s own sweep, diffing `pre-dispatch-status.txt`) can never see what the agents actually did in their ad hoc fallback locations.

## Deliverables
1. Determine empirically whether a Bash-mediated write (`mkdir -p` + redirect, then `rm`) to the `SCRATCH:` path succeeds under a `worktree-always: true` project's main-checkout-anchored `{ctx-dir}`, or whether the guard refuses Bash writes there too.
2. If Bash-mediated writes already succeed: make the `SCRATCH:` dispatch lines in `step3-lens-dispatch.md` and `step3-debate-and-refutation.md` explicitly instruct the Bash-mediated create/delete pattern inline (not just by citing the Scratch rule by reference), so a dispatched agent doesn't need to discover the refusal itself before finding the workaround.
3. If Bash-mediated writes are also refused under `worktree-always`: mint `{ctx-dir}`'s `agent-scratch/` location somewhere genuinely writable under that policy — either inside the dispatching worktree's own gitignored scratch convention (the `.superpowers/` or `.claude-tweaks/scratch/` pattern SDD workspaces already use) or under the session temp root (`_shared/session-tmp-root.md`'s `sessionTmpRoot(sessionId)`, which resolves under `os.tmpdir()` and is therefore outside the repository tree and any worktree-pinning guard entirely).
4. Whichever location fixes it, `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule is updated to state the `worktree-always` case explicitly (it currently documents only the narrower `EnterWorktree`-isolated-dispatch case from #2245), and `bin/build-review-context.js`'s `{ctx-dir}` minting reflects the corrected location.
5. The post-fan-out scratch sweep in `step3-lens-dispatch.md` looks in the corrected location, so it can actually observe what dispatched agents did there.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Given a `worktree-always: true` project, dispatching a Step 3 lens or refutation agent and instructing it to create a probe file at its assigned `SCRATCH:` path succeeds (verified by direct reproduction — either confirming the Bash-mediated pattern now works because it's correctly instructed, or confirming the corrected location is genuinely writable).
2. Given the same setup, the dispatched agent's probe file is visible to the post-fan-out scratch sweep before the agent deletes it (i.e., the sweep's location matches wherever the agent actually wrote).
3. Given the same setup, no dispatched agent needs to fall back to an ad hoc mechanism (a self-created `/tmp` directory, an inline `python -c` probe) to honor the "verify your own work" pattern — the documented `SCRATCH:` mechanism works as instructed.
4. `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule explicitly states the `worktree-always` case's correct mechanism/location, distinguishing it from the pre-existing `EnterWorktree`-isolated-dispatch case if the two turn out to need different handling.
5. A review run under a project WITHOUT `worktree-always` (the case #2245 already covers, presumably already working via the Bash-mediated workaround) is unaffected by this fix — verified by confirming the existing documented behavior for that case still holds.

## Technical Approach
- First, empirically test (in a `worktree-always: true` project or an equivalent simulated environment) whether `mkdir -p {ctx-dir}/agent-scratch/{agent-id} && echo test > {ctx-dir}/agent-scratch/{agent-id}/probe.txt` via Bash succeeds or is refused, to resolve the open question in Current State.
- If refused: change `bin/build-review-context.js`'s `{ctx-dir}` (or specifically the `agent-scratch/` subpath it mints) to resolve under the dispatching worktree's own gitignored scratch convention, or under `_shared/session-tmp-root.md`'s `sessionTmpRoot(sessionId)` — prefer whichever integrates more simply with the existing sweep mechanism in `step3-lens-dispatch.md`.
- If Bash-mediated writes already succeed: add the explicit Bash-mediated instruction inline to the `SCRATCH:` dispatch lines in both `step3-lens-dispatch.md` and `step3-debate-and-refutation.md`, rather than relying on the agent finding and reading `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule on its own after hitting the refusal.
- Update `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule prose to add the `worktree-always` case alongside its existing `EnterWorktree`-isolated-dispatch case.
- Confirm the scratch sweep in `step3-lens-dispatch.md` reads from wherever the corrected `{ctx-dir}` resolves.

### Key Files
- `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md` (line 72) — the `SCRATCH:` dispatch line for lens agents; update per the chosen fix direction.
- `plugin/skills/review/step3-debate-and-refutation.md` (lines 96, 131) — the `SCRATCH:` dispatch lines for refutation/gap-sweep agents; same update.
- `plugin/bin/build-review-context.js` — mints `{ctx-dir}`; change the `agent-scratch/` resolution if the location itself needs to move.
- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — the Scratch rule; add the `worktree-always` case to its existing #2245-documented `EnterWorktree`-isolation case.
- `plugin/skills/_shared/session-tmp-root.md` — candidate target location if the fix needs to move scratch outside the repository tree entirely; `bin/lib/session-tmp.js`'s `sessionTmpRoot`/`sessionTmpPath` are the reusable primitives.

## Gotchas
- Whether Bash-mediated writes are refused under `worktree-always` is the open empirical question this record itself flags — do not assume either answer without testing; the fix direction depends entirely on it (Deliverable 1/2 vs Deliverable 3).
- If the fix moves the scratch location outside `{ctx-dir}`, the post-fan-out scratch sweep (`step3-lens-dispatch.md`) must be updated in the same change — a fix that makes writes succeed but leaves the sweep looking in the old location just changes which half of the contract breaks.
- This is the second report on the same underlying class (#2245 → #2595) — if #2245 is still open or only partially addressed, cross-check before closing either, and prefer consolidating the Scratch rule's documentation into one coherent statement covering both the `EnterWorktree`-isolation case and the `worktree-always` case rather than two disconnected paragraphs.
- `session-tmp.js`'s `sessionTmpRoot` degrades to `null` when `$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` is absent/blank (per `_shared/session-tmp-root.md`'s own degrade rule) — if that path is chosen, the dispatch prompt logic needs a defined fallback for that case too.

## Original request

review step3 dispatch: the SCRATCH path under the main-checkout run dir is unwritable for agents in a worktree-always session (empirical reproduction of closed #2245)

**Summary:** The review procedure hands every dispatched lens/refutation agent a `SCRATCH: {ctx-dir}/agent-scratch/{agent-id}` path under the pipeline run directory, which is anchored under the main checkout - in a `worktree-always` session the PreToolUse guard refuses every write there, so the agents cannot create their scratch, fall back to inline probes, and cannot honour the "delete your scratch before your status word" contract they are told to follow.

**Kind:** Defect

**Affected component:** skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md + step3-debate-and-refutation.md (the `SCRATCH:` dispatch line), bin/build-review-context.js ({ctx-dir} minting), _shared/subagent-output-contract.md (Scratch rule)

**Repro steps:**
1. In a project with `worktree-always: true`, run `/claude-tweaks:flow #N` so `/review` reaches Step 3 with a refutation dispatch (any confirmed lens finding).
2. Read the dispatched agent's reply: it reports that the guard refused every write to the assigned `SCRATCH:` path (`{run-dir}/review-ctx/.../agent-scratch/{id}` under the main checkout).
3. Observe the agent working around it with inline `python -c` probes or a `/tmp` directory it creates and removes itself.

**Expected vs. actual:**
Expected: under `worktree-always`, the agent-scratch directory is minted somewhere the agent can write - inside the worktree's own gitignored scratch area (the `.superpowers/` or `.claude-tweaks/scratch/` convention SDD workspaces already use) or under the session temp root (`_shared/session-tmp-root.md`) - the `SCRATCH:` line names that path, the post-fan-out scratch sweep looks there, and `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s Scratch rule states the worktree case.
Actual: observed 2026-09-18 in a private project on 6.126.0 - both refutation agents reported the refusal and fell back to inline probes (one created and removed a `/tmp` directory). Nothing was lost, but the contract cannot be honoured, each agent spends turns discovering that, and the sweep (`pre-dispatch-status.txt` diff) can never see what they actually did.

**Prior report:** #2245 (closed 2026-09-12) raised this as a plausible, not empirically dispatched, finding on #2022's review; this is the empirical reproduction on 6.126.0 - the refusal is real.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.126.0

groups.title: skills/flow, skills/review: skill guidance doesn't warn dispatched subagents that Monitor/background-task notifications never reach them
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

Pipeline skill guidance that instructs starting a background verification loop or subagent
dispatch and then "waiting for the notification" reads naturally as correct for a top-level
interactive session (where Monitor and background-task completion notifications do arrive) but
does not warn that a dispatched subagent (an `Agent`/`Task`-invoked session) never receives such
notifications the way a top-level session does — waiting there hangs indefinitely with no signal
anything is wrong until an external caller intervenes.

Filed via `/claude-tweaks:feedback` at plugin v6.118.0, citing a harness-level
`contract-violation` event log recording 13+ occurrences of an agent narrating "waiting for the
background task/Monitor notification to arrive" and stopping mid-turn across a single build
phase (main session and multiple dispatched subagents), plus 2 more in a separate review/wrap-up
session for the same unit of work — corrected only when an external coordinator explicitly
stated the limitation. `skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md`'s existing "Hung or non-responsive
single-read agent" section (current build, ~line 50) already covers the adjacent but distinct
case of a *reviewing* agent waiting on a *dispatched* agent that goes silent; it does not cover
this record's scenario — a dispatched subagent itself instructed to background a verification
loop and wait for a notification that will never arrive in its own context.

## Deliverables

- Grep this repo's skill directories fresh at build time for every place a skill instructs
  starting a background verification loop, `Monitor`, or subagent dispatch and then "waiting for
  the notification/completion" — this record's own citations (`skills/flow`, `skills/review`)
  are a starting point, not a guaranteed-current file:line list, since guidance text shifts
  between plugin versions (filed against v6.118.0; current build is newer).
- At each such location, state the limitation once, explicitly, near wherever it first
  introduces Monitor or background-task usage for a verification loop or subagent dispatch: a
  dispatched subagent does not receive Monitor or background-task completion notifications the
  way a top-level session does — run long verification loops in the foreground with a generous
  timeout instead of backgrounding them and waiting for a notification, when running as (or
  dispatching) a subagent.
- Do not duplicate the warning at every call site if a shared `_shared/*.md` fragment already
  covers dispatch mechanics for the affected skills (e.g. `_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md`) —
  add it there once and cite it, per this codebase's own shared-contract-extraction convention,
  if that fragment is already the canonical home for dispatch-mechanics guidance the affected
  skills already cite.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every pipeline skill file that currently instructs backgrounding a verification loop or
  subagent dispatch and waiting for a Monitor/background-task notification carries (directly, or
  via a cited shared fragment) an explicit statement that this pattern does not work inside a
  dispatched subagent's own context.
- The added guidance names the correct alternative for a subagent context: run the verification
  loop in the foreground with a generous timeout, not backgrounded.
- A grep for the current call sites is run and cited in the PR description (or commit message)
  as part of this fix, since this record's own file:line citations may be stale relative to the
  build the fix lands on.

## Technical Approach

1. `grep -rln "Monitor\|background" plugin/skills/flow/ plugin/skills/review/` (and any other
   pipeline skill directory instructing background verification loops or subagent dispatch, per
   the record's "Affected component" note) against the actual build this fix lands on — this
   record's own investigation (at v6.123.0) found no literal "Monitor" or "background" hits in
   `skills/flow/*.md`, and only dispatch-adjacent hits in `skills/review/*.md`
   (`step3-lens-dispatch.md`, `code-mode-steps.md`, `step3-routing.md`,
   `step3-debate-and-refutation.md`) — none of which currently state this specific limitation, so
   the guidance gap this record describes is confirmed still open, just not necessarily at the
   exact file:line the original filing cited.
2. Check whether `_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md` (the shared dispatch-mechanics fragment
   `step3-lens-dispatch.md`'s own header already cites) is the right single home for this
   warning — every pipeline skill dispatching subagents already reads it, so one addition there
   would reach every call site without per-file duplication.
3. Add the warning once, at that shared home (or, if no single shared fragment covers every
   affected call site, at each site directly) — one short paragraph, not a multi-paragraph
   digression.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-dispatch-core.md` — likely single home for the warning, if it
  covers every affected call site
- `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md` — cites the shared fragment; verify coverage
- `plugin/skills/flow/*.md` — re-grep at build time per Technical Approach step 1

## Gotchas

- Do not add this warning as a blanket disclaimer at the top of every pipeline skill — it only
  applies where a skill actually instructs starting a background loop/dispatch and waiting for a
  notification; a skill with no such instruction gets no warning.
- The original filing's file:line citations are from plugin v6.118.0 — verify against the actual
  build this fix lands on before assuming any specific location still matches (see Technical
  Approach step 1).

## Original request

**Summary:** Pipeline skill guidance that instructs starting a background verification loop or subagent dispatch and then "waiting for the notification" does not warn that a dispatched subagent never receives such notifications the way a top-level session does.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** skills/flow, skills/review (and any other pipeline skill instructing background verification loops or subagent dispatch)

**Use case:** Pipeline skills (e.g. `/claude-tweaks:flow`'s polish/re-verify guidance, `/claude-tweaks:review`'s Step 3 dispatch notes) instruct starting a long-running background command or subagent and then "waiting for the notification" -- phrasing that reads naturally as correct guidance for a top-level interactive session, where Monitor and background-task completion notifications do arrive. They do not arrive the same way for a dispatched subagent (an `Agent`/`Task`-invoked session): waiting on one there hangs indefinitely, with no signal that anything is wrong until an external caller intervenes.

This produced a real, repeated, systemic cost on one run I observed, in a private project: the harness's own contract-violation event log recorded 13+ instances of an agent narrating "waiting for the background task/Monitor notification to arrive" and stopping mid-turn across a single build phase (main session and multiple dispatched subagents, none self-corrected mid-run), plus two more in a separate review/wrap-up session for the same unit of work -- corrected only when an external coordinator explicitly stated the limitation. The pattern recurred independently across at least three different agent instances (a build session, its dispatched implementer/reviewer subagents, and a separate review session), all following the same skill-authored background-verification patterns.

**Suggested resolution:** State the limitation once, explicitly, near wherever a pipeline skill first introduces Monitor or background-task usage for a verification loop or subagent dispatch: a dispatched subagent does not receive Monitor or background-task completion notifications the way a top-level session does -- run long verification loops in the foreground with a generous timeout instead of backgrounding them and waiting for a notification, when running as (or dispatching) a subagent.

**Evidence:** A harness-level contract-violation event log recorded 13+ occurrences during a single build phase's own event log, plus 2 more in a separately-run review/wrap-up session against the same unit of work, before an external correction stopped the pattern. Cost: at minimum two full agent turns spent narrating an unresolvable wait before correction; the build-phase recurrence count suggests a materially larger cost there, uncorrected for the run's duration.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.118.0

groups.title: Verify /specify red-team fan-out batching at next live multi-sub-issue run (#649 AC2)
groups.body:
Surface: backend

## Current State

Record #649 added `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s fan-out single-assistant-message-rule
sentence and per-site citations (AC1, fully test-pinned in `tests/subagent-contract-clauses.test.js`,
18/18 passing). AC2 — "A `/specify` red-team over 2+ `ceremony:standard` sub-issues launches its
personas in ≤ (number of sub-issues) assistant messages, verified in the transcript by `Agent`
tool_use blocks sharing a message id" — is a live-behavior criterion that cannot be verified by a
static `node --test` assertion; it can only be confirmed by observing an actual future `/specify`
decomposition run's transcript.

## Deliverables

Confirm, at the next `/specify` decomposition run over 2+ `ceremony:standard` sub-issues, that
persona dispatch actually batches into ≤N assistant messages per `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s
fan-out single-assistant-message rule and `red-team.md`'s per-sub-issue batching unit. Record the
observation (transcript excerpt or note) against this item, or file a defect against
`red-team.md`'s dispatch prose if it does not.

## Acceptance Criteria

A `/specify` run over 2+ `ceremony:standard` sub-issues is observed; its persona `Agent` tool_use
calls are confirmed (via transcript `tool_use` block message-id grouping) to arrive in ≤ (number of
sub-issues) assistant messages.

## Technical Approach

Wait for (or trigger) a `/claude-tweaks:specify` decomposition-mode run that produces 2 or more
`ceremony:standard` sub-issue records — `ceremony-check` (`assess-agent-autonomy/ceremony-check.md`)
resolves the tier per sub-issue during that run's own Step 3, so the tier isn't knowable until the
run happens. Once such a run occurs, inspect that session's stored transcript for the Step 5
red-team dispatch (`specify/red-team.md`'s Parallel dispatch section): locate the `Agent` tool_use
blocks for each dispatched persona and group them by the assistant message id each block belongs
to. Confirm the number of distinct assistant message ids covering all persona dispatches for a
given sub-issue is ≤ the number of sub-issues in that batch. Use the same read-only transcript
inspection method `transcript-payload-verification` documents for reading this session's own
locally-stored transcript, rather than instrumenting or modifying `red-team.md` itself.

If the count exceeds the bound, file a defect issue against `red-team.md`'s dispatch prose
(quoting the transcript grouping that violates the rule) instead of editing the file directly from
this record — this record's own deliverable is the observation, not the fix.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/specify/red-team.md` — the per-sub-issue persona dispatch procedure being observed
- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — the fan-out single-assistant-message rule this observation verifies compliance with
- `tests/subagent-contract-clauses.test.js` — AC1's existing static test coverage (unaffected by this record)

## Gotchas

- This record's acceptance criterion depends on an external event (a live `/specify` decomposition
  run over 2+ `ceremony:standard` sub-issues happening) that this record cannot itself trigger on a
  fixed schedule — it may sit open for some time until a qualifying run occurs naturally, or until
  someone deliberately runs one to close it out.
- A qualifying run must be observed via its own transcript at the time it happens; this record
  cannot be resolved from historical data if no already-completed run's transcript is still
  available.

## Original request

Verify /specify red-team fan-out batching at next live multi-sub-issue run (#649 AC2)

Origin: ledger resolve gate

groups.title: plan-authoring-checks: add a consumer-enumeration check (pick-one vs list-all) for tasks that change how rows of a shared table are selected
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` is a catalogue of bold-paragraph prose checks (return-shape widening, blocking-verification-downgrade, deictic-reference re-resolution, verbatim-command run-once, degrade-clause convention, copied-config re-derivation, renumbering-completeness, batched-plan marker, behavioral-claim, byte-pin, consumer-timing, gate-over-producers, sole-site-and-producer-side, real-input probe, independent-count) that a plan author consults during `/claude-tweaks:build` Spec Step 3 / Design Step 3. None of the existing checks asks the author to enumerate every consumer of a reader when a plan task changes which rows of a shared table or frame that reader returns (a dedup rule, an ordering the caller relies on, an "effective row" rule). This gap let a real defect through: a 2026-09-18 incident where an append-only versions table held each key twice after a migration appended a migrated twin beside the original row; the plan framed the fix as "readers pick the wrong twin" and ordered the twins newest-first, but one consumer (an admin API endpoint) lists and resolves every returned row rather than picking one, so it kept raising on the un-migrated twin (HTTP 500 on every migrated entity) after the ordering fix shipped. Only the whole-branch review's architecture lens caught it, costing a fix-now wave (two implementer rounds, one scoped review, one full re-verification, ~25 minutes).

## Deliverables
1. A new bold-paragraph prose check in `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md`, titled **Consumer-enumeration check**, phrased in the same style as its neighboring checks in that file: when a plan task changes which rows of a shared table or frame a reader returns (a dedup, an ordering a caller relies on, an "effective row" rule), the plan must enumerate every consumer of that reader (grep for the reader's name and for direct reads of the underlying table) and classify each consumer as *pick-one* (an ordering fix suffices) or *list-all* (needs an explicit collapse/dedup, not just an ordering). The classification goes in the task's Files/Interfaces block; a list-all consumer with no collapse step in any task is a plan defect this check exists to catch.
2. A cross-reference from `plugin/skills/build/plan-audit.md`'s Check B guidance (the `Scope keywords:` fs-walk section) pointing at the new consumer-enumeration check, so a plan author is reminded that `Scope keywords:` can carry the reader's name and Check B's fs-walk will surface consumer files the plan's task list omitted.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` contains a new bold-paragraph check titled "Consumer-enumeration check" using the pick-one / list-all vocabulary, phrased and formatted consistently with its neighboring checks (a bold lead-in sentence naming the trigger condition, followed by the required plan-author action and the consequence of skipping it).
2. The new paragraph states explicitly that the consumer classification (pick-one vs. list-all) belongs in the task's Files/Interfaces block, and that an unclassified list-all consumer is a plan defect.
3. `plugin/skills/build/plan-audit.md`'s Check B section (or its neighboring prose) gains a cross-reference to the new check, naming that `Scope keywords:` can include the reader's name so the fs-walk surfaces consumers the plan's task list omitted.
4. A plan whose task changes a reader's row-selection behavior (ordering, dedup, "effective row" rule) but whose Files/Interfaces block names no pick-one/list-all classification is inconsistent with the new check — i.e., the check's own text makes this failure mode identifiable to a plan self-review or a future mechanized Check.

## Technical Approach
Add the new check as a new bold-paragraph entry in `plan-authoring-checks.md`, following the existing convention: bold check name, one paragraph describing the trigger condition (a plan task changing row-selection behavior of a shared reader), the required author action (enumerate consumers via grep, classify each pick-one/list-all, record classification in Files/Interfaces), and the failure mode it catches (an unclassified list-all consumer). Optionally cite the 2026-09-18 incident pattern as the motivating example, matching how neighboring checks (e.g. the Gate-over-producers check, the Sole-site-and-producer-side check) cite real incidents with measured cost. Then add a short cross-reference sentence in `plan-audit.md`'s Check B section noting the new check and that `Scope keywords:` can name the reader to let the fs-walk surface its consumers.

### Key Files
- `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` — add the new "Consumer-enumeration check" bold paragraph, following the file's existing per-check convention
- `plugin/skills/build/plan-audit.md` — add a cross-reference in or near the Check B guidance section pointing at the new check and its `Scope keywords:` usage

## Gotchas
This check joins the file's other judgment-only checks (per `plan-audit.md`'s own framing: "Judgment checks ... stay prose in `plan-authoring.md` — they are not mechanically checkable") — it is not proposed as a new mechanized Check A-E in `plan-audit.js`, only as prose guidance a plan author and a plan self-review consult. Keep the new paragraph's phrasing consistent with the file's established voice (each existing check opens with a bold check name followed by "when ... check/flag/enumerate/name" imperative framing) rather than introducing a different structure.

## Original request

plan-authoring-checks: add a consumer-enumeration check (pick-one vs list-all) for tasks that change how rows of a shared table are selected

**Summary:** `plan-authoring-checks.md` has no check for a task that changes how rows of a shared table are selected (dedup, ordering, an "effective row" rule) - nothing forces the plan to enumerate every consumer of that reader and classify it as pick-one (an ordering suffices) or list-all (needs a collapse), so a list-all consumer is missed by an ordering-only fix until the whole-branch review.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md (plan-authoring checks run by /claude-tweaks:build Spec Step 3 / Design Step 3)

**Use case:**
Observed 2026-09-18 in a private project: an append-only versions table held each key twice after a migration appended a migrated twin beside the original row. The record and the plan framed the fix as "readers pick the wrong twin" and listed the store's history reader among the pickers, so the plan ordered the twins newest-first and stopped. One consumer of that reader, an admin API endpoint, lists and resolves every returned row; ordering left it raising on the un-migrated twin (HTTP 500 on every migrated entity). Only the whole-branch review's architecture lens found it, at the cost of a fix-now wave (two implementer rounds, one scoped review, one full re-verification, roughly 25 minutes). Nothing at plan-authoring time asked which consumers list rather than pick.

Proposed:
- A new bold paragraph in `plan-authoring-checks.md`: **Consumer-enumeration check** - when a plan task changes which rows of a shared table or frame a reader returns (a dedup, an ordering a caller relies on, an "effective row" rule), the plan must enumerate every consumer of that reader (grep for the reader's name and for direct reads of the table) and classify each as *pick-one* or *list-all*; the classification goes in the task's Files/Interfaces block, and a list-all consumer with no collapse in any task is a plan defect.
- Reference the check from `plan-audit.md`'s Check B guidance so `Scope keywords:` can carry the reader's name and the fs-walk surfaces consumers the plan omitted.

Acceptance: the new paragraph exists, phrased like its neighbours, with the pick-one / list-all vocabulary; a plan whose task changes a reader's ordering but whose Files/Interfaces block names no consumer classification fails the plan self-review.

**Definition:** Clear

groups.title: plan-audit Check C: executes a `git stash push` found in Step 2 prose - the Run: extractor takes the first backticked span with no VCS-mutation refusal
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`bin/plan-audit.js`'s Check C (`bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js`'s `checkC`) pre-runs each task's Step 2 verification command against the live repo to confirm it currently fails (per `plan-audit.md`'s documented contract that Check C is read-only). The command is extracted by `bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js`'s `extractStep2Verification`, which matches `/^Run:\s*(.+)$/m` anywhere within the Step 2 window — not anchored to the heading itself — then takes the **first backticked span** found on that matched line as the command to run (`parser.js` lines 102-107):

```js
const runMatch = window.match(/^Run:\s*(.+)$/m);
...
const backtickedCmd = runMatch[1].match(/`([^`]+)`/);
const command = (backtickedCmd ? backtickedCmd[1] : runMatch[1]).trim();
```

This means any line starting with `Run:` inside the Step 2 window — including a prose line that merely *mentions* a command in prose, such as `Run: never run \`git stash push -u -m tag\` here; use a WIP commit instead` — gets its first backticked span extracted and executed verbatim as the verification command by `checkC` (`checks.js` line 192: `const { exitCode, output } = run(command, repoRoot);`). `checkC` performs no inspection of `command` before executing it — there is no check anywhere in the current code for VCS-mutating commands (`git stash`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git reset`, `git checkout`, `git switch`, `git clean`, `git rebase`, `git merge`, `gh` writes, or any compound form via `&&`/`;`/`|`).

This was observed in production on 2026-09-18 (plugin 6.126.0): a plan's Step 2 prose contained the phrase above, `checkC` executed the extracted `git stash push -u -m tag` against the live worktree, and an untracked plan file was swept off the shared stash stack — the same stash stack every worktree and sibling session shares. Recovery required a manual `git stash apply <sha>`, a drop-by-tag, and a plan rewrite removing the phrase. `plan-audit.md` documents Check C as read-only; this is a violation of that documented contract, not new intended behavior.

## Deliverables
1. `extractStep2Verification` (or a new validation step downstream of it) identifies a genuine verification command — either a fenced ` ```Run:``` `-style code block, or a `Run:` line whose backticked span is the *entire* remainder of the line after `Run:` (i.e., the line is `Run: \`{command}\`` with nothing else) — and treats any other shape (prose containing a `Run:`-prefixed line with an embedded backticked span that isn't the whole remainder) as unparseable, not as an extractable command.
2. `checkC` refuses to execute any extracted command whose first token, or any token immediately following a `&&`, `;`, or `|` segment separator, is a VCS-mutation verb: `git stash`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git reset`, `git checkout`, `git switch`, `git clean`, `git rebase`, `git merge`, or any `gh` subcommand that writes (`gh issue create/edit/close`, `gh pr create/merge/close`, etc. — the write-vs-read split `gh-api-module-pattern` skill or existing `gh` write-detection logic in the repo already draws, reused rather than redefined here).
3. A refused command is reported under the audit's `warnings` output (not `findings` — it isn't a task-verification result, it's a check-mechanism refusal), naming the task, the refused command, and the reason (VCS-mutation refusal).
4. The audit summary lists every command Check C actually executed, so a reader can confirm what ran without needing to reproduce the audit.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Given a plan whose Task N Step 2 window contains `Run: never run \`git stash push -u -m tag\` here; use a WIP commit instead` followed by an `Expected: FAIL` line, running `node bin/plan-audit.js <plan-file>` does NOT execute `git stash push -u -m tag` against the repo — `git stash list` before and after the audit run is unchanged.
2. Given the same plan, the audit's `warnings` output includes an entry for Task N naming the refused command and a VCS-mutation-refusal reason (not a generic "unparseable" reason, since the extraction pattern technically matched — this is a refusal, not a parse failure).
3. Given a plan whose Task N Step 2 has a genuine verification command in the correct shape (`Run: \`npm test -- path/to/test.js\`` as the entire remainder of the line, or an equivalent fenced block), `checkC` still executes that command exactly as it does today — the fix does not regress the legitimate pre-run path.
4. Given a plan whose Step 2 verification command is a compound shell command with a VCS-mutation verb after a `&&`/`;`/`|` (e.g. `npm test && git commit -am wip`), Check C refuses the whole command — the per-segment check catches mutation verbs that aren't the first token of the whole line.
5. The audit's output (whatever format it currently renders — findings/warnings/summary) lists every command Check C executed during that run, for at least the passing case in AC 3.
6. A plan whose Step 2 verification command is a non-VCS, non-mutating command (e.g. `npm test`, `node script.js`) continues to execute and produce findings exactly as before — the fix is scoped to VCS/gh-write mutation verbs, not a general command whitelist that would break existing passing plans.

## Technical Approach
- In `bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js`'s `extractStep2Verification`, tighten the `Run:` line match so that a backticked span is only treated as the command when it is the entire remainder of the `Run:` line (after trimming) — i.e., `runMatch[1].trim()` equals the backticked span itself (including its backticks) — or when the verification is expressed as a fenced code block under the `Run:` label. A `Run:` line whose backticked span is only part of a longer prose sentence should return `null` (or a distinct "prose, not a command" signal) rather than extracting the first backtick match.
- In `bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js`'s `checkC`, before calling `run(command, repoRoot)`, tokenize `command` by shell segment separators (`&&`, `;`, `|`) and check each segment's first token against a VCS-mutation verb list (`git stash|commit|push|reset|checkout|switch|clean|rebase|merge`, `gh` write subcommands). On a match, skip execution for that check and push an entry to a new `warnings`-shaped refusal record instead of calling `run`.
- Extend `checkC`'s return shape to carry the list of executed commands (for the audit summary requirement, AC 5) alongside the existing `findings`/`warnings`/`appendShaped`.
- Reuse any existing gh-write-detection logic already in the repo (check `bin/lib/issues/github-write-transport.md`'s described split, or similar, before hand-rolling a new gh-write verb list) rather than inventing a second classification of "which gh subcommands write."

### Key Files
- `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js` — `extractStep2Verification` (lines 93-108); tighten the backtick-extraction condition per Deliverable 1.
- `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js` — `checkC` (lines 176-214); add the VCS-mutation refusal check before `run(command, repoRoot)` is called, and extend the return shape to list executed commands.
- `plugin/skills/plan-audit.md` (or wherever the Check C contract prose lives — confirm exact path) — already documents Check C as read-only; verify no wording change needed, since this fix restores rather than changes the documented contract.
- `plugin/bin/plan-audit.js` — CLI entry point; confirm the audit summary rendering picks up the new executed-commands list.

## Gotchas
- The VCS-mutation verb list must be conservative but complete enough to catch the incident class described — a partial list that misses e.g. `git rm` or `git tag -d` leaves the same class of destructive-mutation risk open. Cross-check against any existing mutation-verb list elsewhere in the repo (hooks, other guards) before finalizing this one, to avoid two divergent lists.
- Tightening `extractStep2Verification`'s match condition (Deliverable 1) risks making some currently-working plans' genuinely-intended `Run:` lines newly unparseable if their formatting is looser than assumed (e.g. trailing whitespace or a trailing comment after the backticked command) — verify against a sample of real existing plans before landing, and prefer a targeted fix (distinguishing "backtick is the whole line" from "backtick is embedded in a longer sentence") over an overly strict pattern.
- The compound-command per-segment check (Deliverable 2/AC 4) needs to handle shell quoting correctly — a VCS verb appearing inside a quoted string argument (not as an actual command token) must not trigger a false refusal; a naive string-split on `&&`/`;`/`|` risks this edge case for quoted arguments containing those characters.
- This bug represents a real security/safety gap (arbitrary destructive command execution from plan file content) with production impact already observed — treat the fix as data-loss-prevention-critical, not a cosmetic parser tweak.

## Original request

plan-audit Check C: executes a `git stash push` found in Step 2 prose - the Run: extractor takes the first backticked span with no VCS-mutation refusal

**Summary:** `plan-audit.js` Check C ran a `git stash push -u -m ...` that a plan's Step 2 prose mentioned as *forbidden* - the Step 2 extractor takes the first backticked span on a `Run:` line as the verification command and executes it with no VCS-mutation refusal, sweeping an untracked plan file off the shared stash stack mid-build.

**Kind:** Defect

**Affected component:** bin/plan-audit.js Check C (bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js `extractStep2Verification`, bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js)

**Repro steps:**
1. Write a plan whose Task N Step 2 window contains a line such as `Run: never run \`git stash push -u -m tag\` here; use a WIP commit instead` (prose with a backticked command that is not the verification command), followed by an `Expected: FAIL` line.
2. Run `node bin/plan-audit.js <plan-file>` in a worktree whose repo has an untracked file.
3. Observe `git stash list`: a new entry exists and the untracked file is gone from the working tree; the audit report shows nothing beyond a Check C result.

**Expected vs. actual:**
Expected: Check C is read-only, as `plan-audit.md` states - it pre-runs only a genuine verification command (a fenced `Run:` block or a `Run:` line whose backticked span is the whole remainder), refuses any command whose first token (or any `&&`/`;`/`|` segment's first token) is a VCS mutation (`git stash/commit/push/reset/checkout/switch/clean/rebase/merge`, `gh` writes), reports the refusal under `warnings`, and lists every command it executed in the audit summary.
Actual: `extractStep2Verification` matches `^Run:` anywhere in the Step 2 window, takes the first backticked span on that line, and `checks.js` executes it as-is. Observed 2026-09-18 in a private project on 6.126.0: the stash ran on the stack shared by every worktree and sibling session; recovery needed a manual `git stash apply <sha>` plus drop-by-tag and a plan rewrite removing the phrase.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.126.0

groups.title: plan-authoring-checks: add an upstream-schema premise check — a spec claim about a third-party schema semantic must be proven from that schema DDL/migration, not restated
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` documents a fixed set of prose checks run during Spec Step 3 / Design Step 3 plan finalization — the Behavioral-claim check (line 21), the Verbatim-command run-once check (line 11), the Real-input probe check (line 31), and others, each targeting a failure mode that "reads as correct to a task-level review that only compares plan text against implemented code" (line 3's framing). None of the existing checks cover a premise about a schema this project does not own: a claim like "flag X on table Y means Z" or "column C is the owner" that names semantics of a third-party/upstream schema.

Observed 2026-09-17 in a private project: a record asserted that a per-item flag in an upstream migration's link table reproduced old single-owner semantics, and cited the migration file by path. The plan restated this as a Global Constraint. `plan-audit.js` passed, two implementers and two task reviews executed it faithfully — every reviewer compared plan text against implemented code and found agreement, because the premise itself was never checked against the upstream DDL. Only the whole-branch review, which opened the migration's actual seed and index definitions, found the filter dropped every attached-but-not-current row, exposing a green pipeline that would have silently under-populated its artifact. This cost a fix wave across reader, fixtures, tests, skill, and spec, plus a cancelled and re-dispatched remote test suite.

`plan-audit.js`'s `checkB` (`plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js:110`) already consumes `extractScopeKeywords` (`plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js:64`) to validate a plan's declared file scope against its planned edits — this is the established mechanized-check pattern a new `Premise-refs:` field would extend, rather than a novel audit mechanism.

## Deliverables

1. A new bold-paragraph prose check in `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md`, following the file's existing convention (a **Bold check name:** paragraph stating the rule, its rationale, and a worked incident) — the "Upstream-schema premise check": when a spec or plan asserts a semantic about a schema this project does not own (a flag's meaning, a column's role, what a seed/backfill writes, which index enforces uniqueness), the plan must cite the DDL, migration, or model definition that proves it — read at authoring time, with the relevant line quoted — or mark the sentence `unverified`.
2. The new paragraph is listed alongside the file's other checks wherever Spec Step 3 / Design Step 3 point at this file (the same reference sites the existing checks already rely on — no separate cross-reference list to maintain, per this file's own convention of being the single citable source for these checks).
3. A `Premise-refs:` field addition to `plan-audit.js`'s Check B / Scope-keyword extraction (`extractScopeKeywords`, `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js:64`): a plan may declare `Premise-refs: {path or URL}` lines naming what it claims to have read; `checkB` (`plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js:110`) reports any that do not resolve to an existing path (or, for a URL, is left unverified — Check B has no network access, so a URL reference is recorded but not fetched).

## Acceptance Criteria

- `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` contains a new bold paragraph titled "Upstream-schema premise check" following the file's existing paragraph structure (bold name, rule statement, rationale sentence, worked incident).
- The new paragraph names the archetype from the observed incident (a per-item vs. per-resource flag mix-up) as its worked example, consistent with every other check in the file citing a real incident.
- `extractScopeKeywords` (`plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js:64`) recognizes a `Premise-refs:` line and returns the listed paths/URLs as a distinct field, verified by a unit test with a plan fixture containing `Premise-refs:` lines.
- `checkB` (`plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js:110`) reports any `Premise-refs:` path that does not resolve to an existing file in the repo, verified by a unit test with a fixture naming a nonexistent path.
- `checkB` does not report a `Premise-refs:` URL as unresolved in the same way a bad path is — Check B has no network access, so a URL is recorded as present but explicitly not fetch-verified (documented distinction, tested by a fixture asserting the URL case does not trip the same failure branch as the missing-path case).
- A plan fixture with no `Premise-refs:` field at all continues to pass `checkB` unchanged (backward compatible — the field is optional, not mandatory) — verified by re-running the existing `checkB` test suite unmodified.
- `npm test` passes in full after the change.

## Technical Approach

Add the new prose paragraph to `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md`, matching the file's established structure: a bold check name, the rule (what a plan-authoring pass must do), a one-sentence rationale tying it to the file's shared framing (task-level review agreement without a mechanism check), and the 2026-09-17 incident as the worked example, with the observed archetype (per-item vs. per-resource flag) named explicitly as the acceptance names it.

Extend `extractScopeKeywords` in `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js` to recognize a `Premise-refs:` line (following whatever line-prefix parsing convention the function already uses for its other scope keywords) and return the listed references as a new field on its result object. Extend `checkB` in `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js` to accept that new field, checking each named path with a filesystem existence check (matching the pattern the function already uses for planned-file validation) and reporting a distinct failure category for unresolved paths — separate from Check B's existing unplanned-file failure category, since these are semantically different findings (a scope mismatch vs. an unverifiable citation).

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` — add the new "Upstream-schema premise check" bold paragraph, following the file's existing structure and citing the 2026-09-17 incident.
- `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/parser.js` — extend `extractScopeKeywords` (line 64) to parse an optional `Premise-refs:` field.
- `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/checks.js` — extend `checkB` (line 110) to validate `Premise-refs:` paths against the filesystem and report unresolved ones as a distinct failure category.
- `plugin/bin/plan-audit.js` — confirm the CLI's summary output (line 34's `Check B: {n} unplanned file(s)` pattern) extends to report the new unresolved-premise-ref category distinctly, not folded into the existing unplanned-file count.
- Existing `checkB`/`extractScopeKeywords` test files under `tests/` (locate via the same directory `plugin/bin/lib/plan-audit/` tests live alongside, per this repo's `tests/bin-lib/{module}` convention) — extend with fixtures covering the new field.

## Gotchas

- `plan-audit.js` runs statically over plan text — it cannot itself open and read the cited upstream DDL/migration to verify the *content* of the claim, only that the cited path exists. The mechanized half of this check (`Premise-refs:` resolution) is a citation-presence check, not a semantic verifier; the semantic verification (does the cited line actually say what the plan claims) stays a human/reviewer judgment at authoring time, per the prose check's own instruction to quote the relevant line.
- A URL reference in `Premise-refs:` cannot be verified by Check B (no network access) — this must be documented as an explicit limitation in both the prose check and the mechanized check's own output, not silently treated the same as a missing local path.
- The new field is optional; a plan that asserts no third-party schema semantics has nothing to declare, and `checkB` must not require the field to be present in general — only validate it when it is.
- Distinguish the new "unresolved premise reference" failure category from Check B's existing "unplanned file" category in both the check's return shape and the CLI's summary text, so a plan author isn't left guessing which of two different findings a given failure line refers to.

## Original request

plan-authoring-checks: add an upstream-schema premise check — a spec claim about a third-party schema semantic must be proven from that schema DDL/migration, not restated

**Summary:** `plan-authoring-checks.md` has no check that forces a plan to prove a claim about a *third-party* schema's semantics from that schema's own DDL/migration — a wrong premise about an upstream flag survived specify, plan authoring, plan-audit and two task reviews, and was caught only by the whole-branch review.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** build/plan-authoring-checks.md (Spec Step 3 / plan-audit)

**Use case:**
`plan-authoring-checks.md` has the behavioral-claim check (a plan sentence asserting a runtime effect must name the code path that produces it) and the verbatim-command check (run a dictated command once against the live target), but nothing covers a premise about a schema this project does not own: "flag X on table Y means Z", "column C is the owner", "the seed sets D for every attached row". Such a premise arrives in the record body, is copied into the plan's Global Constraints and the implementer's brief, and every task review agrees with it because both sides restate it — only a reviewer who opens the upstream DDL can falsify it.

Observed 2026-09-17 in a private project: an upstream service's migration renamed a lookup table and moved its item link into a link table with two partial unique indexes (one per-resource "live link", one per-item "current" flag). The record asserted that the per-item flag reproduced the old single-owner semantics and even cited the migration file by path; the plan restated it as a Global Constraint; `plan-audit.js` passed; two implementers and two task reviews executed it faithfully; the whole-branch review read the migration's seed and index definitions and found the filter dropped every attached-but-not-current row — a green pipeline that would have silently under-populated its artifact. groups.title: plan-audit: a plan whose inline test contradicts its inline implementation passes every pre-dispatch check
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`/claude-tweaks:build` Spec Step 3 writes a plan whose tasks carry both the complete test code (Step 1) and the complete implementation (Step 3). `bin/plan-audit.js` Check C pre-runs each task's Step 2 `Run:`/`Expected: FAIL` command against the *current* repo, and `skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md` lists judgment checks, but nothing exercises the plan's own inline test text against the plan's own inline implementation text. A plan can therefore ship a test asserting that a given phrase is absent from a command's stdout beside a script that unconditionally emits that same phrase on that same path — a self-contradictory plan that nonetheless passes plan authoring, `plan-audit.js`, and dispatch. Observed on a pipeline run 2026-09-17 in a private project: this exact contradiction survived every pre-dispatch check and was caught only when the Task 2 implementer's GREEN run failed, requiring one implementer detour and one controller ruling (a `Ruling:` in the SDD ledger) to determine which side of the plan was authoritative.

## Deliverables
1. Add a plan-authoring check (prose, in `skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md`): "Inline self-consistency — when a task's Step 1 and Step 3 both inline complete code, run the inlined test against the inlined implementation in a scratch directory before finalizing the plan; a red result is a plan defect to fix at authoring time, not a dispatch-time surprise."
2. (Optional, if scoped in during build) a mechanized Check E in `bin/plan-audit.js`: for a task whose Step 1 and Step 3 code fences name the same `Test:`/`Create:` paths, materialize both into a temp tree and run the task's Step 4 `Run:` command there; report `checkE.ok` and the failing region, following the same reporting shape Check C already uses.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A plan whose inlined test asserts the absence of a substring that the inlined implementation always emits is flagged before dispatch — either by the prose check surfacing it during the authoring pass, or by Check E's automated result when Deliverable 2 is implemented.
- A plan with no inlined code, or whose Step 4 command cannot run in a scratch tree (e.g. it imports files outside the plan's own listed files), is reported as "not checked" rather than failed or silently skipped.
- The existing Check A-D behavior in `bin/plan-audit.js` is unchanged — verified by running the existing `plan-audit.js` test suite before and after this change and confirming no regressions.
- If Check E (Deliverable 2) is implemented, it follows Check C's existing reporting shape (`checkE.ok` plus a failing-region citation) so callers reading `plan-audit.js`'s output can handle it uniformly with the other checks.

## Technical Approach
Deliverable 1 is a documentation-only prose addition to `skills/build/plan-authoring-checks.md`, instructing the plan-authoring agent to self-test inline code pairs in a scratch directory before finalizing the plan. ## Gotchas
- Check E (if built) must correctly identify when Step 1/Step 3 code fences reference the *same* file paths — a task whose test and implementation touch different files entirely is out of scope for this check and must report "not checked," not a false positive.
- Materializing inline code into a scratch tree and running it risks reproducing whatever caused the original contradiction (e.g. hidden dependencies on the current repo state) — keep the scratch tree isolated the same way Check C's existing pre-run isolation already works, don't invent a new isolation mechanism.
