groups.title: flaky.js's allowlist match is exact-string only — doesn't reuse verify-scope.json's own glob engine
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`bin/lib/verify/flaky.js`'s `planRetry` builds `new Set(flaky.files)` and treats a failing file as allowlisted only when `listed.has(file)` — exact string equality against the declaration's `flaky.files` entries. The same `verify-scope.json` file's `rules[].match` entries are globs, compiled by `bin/lib/issues/blast-radius.js`'s `globToRegExp` (memoized, `**` spans segments, `*` stays segment-bound, every other character escaped) and applied in `scope.js`. So one schema carries two matching semantics: a project can write `tests/**` in a rule but must enumerate `tests/flaky/a.test.js`, `tests/flaky/b.test.js`, … in the allowlist and edit the list every time a flaky file is added. `declaration.js` validates `flaky.files` only as "an array of path strings", and `test/verification.md`'s Flake handling paragraph documents the entries as "exact repo-relative paths" that "must match the failing-file paths exactly as the suite's own output prints them".

## Deliverables
- [ ] `planRetry` matches each failing file against `flaky.files` with `globToRegExp(entry).test(file)` (any entry matching allowlists the file), keeping the `unlisted: [...]` reason and the fail-safe on any unmatched file; an entry with no glob metacharacter compiles to an anchored literal, so existing exact-path lists behave byte-for-byte as today.
- [ ] `declaration.js`'s `flaky.files` validation message reads "an array of path or glob strings"; no schema change.
- [ ] `test/verification.md`'s Flake handling paragraph: "exact repo-relative paths" becomes "repo-relative paths or globs (the same `**`/`*` forms `rules[].match` accepts)", and the sentence that entries must match the suite's printed paths keeps its warning about package-relative output — a glob is matched against the same printed path.
- [ ] Tests in `tests/bin-lib/verify/flaky.test.js`: a `tests/flaky/**` entry allowlists a new file under that directory; an exact entry still matches only itself; `tests/*.test.js` does not match a nested file (segment-bound `*`); an entry that matches nothing leaves the unlisted reason naming the file. `tests/bin-lib/verify/declaration.test.js` gets the message text update if it pins the old wording.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Existing exact-path `flaky.files` entries produce the same `planRetry` decisions as before (the existing flaky cases pass unmodified).
2. A glob entry allowlists every failing file it matches, with `**` and `*` behaving exactly as they do for `rules[].match`.
3. A failing file matched by no entry still blocks the retry with `unlisted:` naming it.
4. The `flakyHits` counter and the `flaky-allowlist` escalation CAVEAT stay keyed by the concrete file path, never by the glob; `npm test` is green.

## Technical Approach
Reuse the engine the file already shares a schema with: `scope.js` imports `globToRegExp` from `bin/lib/issues/blast-radius.js`; `flaky.js` imports the same function and replaces the `Set` lookup with a `some(entry => globToRegExp(entry).test(file))` pass. The regex builder escapes every non-glob character, so backward compatibility for exact paths is a property of the compiler, not a special case. The retry command template still substitutes the concrete file, so nothing downstream sees a glob.

### Key Files
- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/flaky.js` — `planRetry` (the `listed` Set and `unlisted` filter).
- `plugin/bin/lib/issues/blast-radius.js` — `globToRegExp` (read-only, imported).
- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/declaration.js` — `flaky.files` validation message.
- `plugin/skills/test/verification.md` — Flake handling paragraph.
- `tests/bin-lib/verify/flaky.test.js`, `tests/bin-lib/verify/declaration.test.js`.

## Gotchas
- `globToRegExp` has no `?` wildcard (it escapes `?`); say "the same forms `rules[].match` accepts" rather than promising full glob syntax.
- The escalation counter is what tells a maintainer which concrete file keeps flaking; a glob allowlist must not blur that, so the per-file `flakyHits` key is unchanged and the `flaky-allowlist` CAVEAT still names the file.
- `/claude-tweaks:wrap-up`'s leftover routing files an escalation as a backlog record per file; a glob entry does not change that shape.

## Original request
Found by the pre-v6.119.0 whole-branch review (range e7d6d9331..4db32e020).

Defer-reason: tangential

groups.title: verification.md's isolate-and-rerun-once rule has no procedure for a no-parse test failure
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`plugin/skills/test/verification.md`'s "Flake handling (tests check only)" section makes the runner the owner of listed-flaky retries (#1925) and keeps one agent-performed isolation step for a failure in an **unlisted** file: re-run that one file (`node --test path/to/file.test.js`), isolated pass → flake, isolated fail → regression. That step presupposes a file name. `bin/lib/verify/flaky.js`'s `planRetry` returns `{ retry: false, reason: 'no-parse' }` when `extractFailingFiles` yields nothing (`sniffFamily` classified the output as `generic`, or the family's failing-file pattern did not match), and `bin/verify.js` records that decision without acting on it; the prose has no branch for it, so a `no-parse` failure is presented as a flat regression with no flake adjudication. Before #1925, the isolate-and-rerun-once rule was unconditional.

"Isolating pre-existing failures by file, not by keyword grep" (the section above the flake handling) is the other half of the same rule and likewise assumes extractable paths. `report.json`'s check entry already carries the retry decision as `retryDecision` (`{ retry: false, reason: 'no-parse' | 'unlisted: […]' | 'no-template' | 'max-retries-0' | 'unreadable-log' }`, written by `verify.js` and carried by `report.js`), so the signal the prose needs exists; nothing in the prose or the stdout summary reads it.

## Deliverables

- [ ] **Two named isolation paths.** `verification.md`'s Flake handling section states them explicitly: **named-file isolation** (today's unlisted-file rule, unchanged) and **whole-suite re-run** for a `no-parse` failure: re-run the `tests` check once through the runner (`node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/verify.js" --cmd tests="{command}"` with the same scope and `--no-stamp`-equivalent posture so a second pass never records a pass stamp on its own), then adjudicate: second run passes → **flake** (reported exactly as the named-file flake is, verdict unchanged); fails again → **regression**. One re-run, never more; the whole-suite cost is stated as the reason this path is the fallback, not the default.
- [ ] **The prose and the summary read the existing decision.** `verification.md` tells the agent to read `retryDecision.reason` from `report.json` (`no-parse` → whole-suite path; an `unlisted:` reason → named-file path) instead of re-deriving the extractor's outcome; `bin/verify.js`'s stdout summary for a failed `tests` check gains the clause `(retry: no-parse — whole-suite re-run applies)` so the path is visible without opening the report.
- [ ] **Pre-existing-failures section cross-reference.** "Isolating pre-existing failures by file" gains one sentence pointing at the whole-suite path for output with no extractable paths, so the two sections agree.
- [ ] **Tests.** `tests/bin-lib/verify/cli.test.js`: stdout carries the no-parse clause for a generic-family failing fixture and no clause for a passing check; the existing `retryDecision` report cases stay unchanged. A prose pin (sized like `tests/verify-scope-declaration.test.js`) asserting the two path names and the one-re-run cap in `verification.md`.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `verification.md` names both isolation paths, the `no-parse` trigger, the single whole-suite re-run, and the flake/regression adjudication for it; the named-file paragraph is byte-identical to today apart from the new heading.
2. `verification.md` names `retryDecision.reason` as the selector between the two paths; the stdout summary shows the no-parse clause for a `no-parse` failure and nothing for a passing check.
3. A generic-family failing fixture run through `verify.js` twice, with the second run passing, is adjudicated as a flake by the documented procedure and never records a pass stamp from the re-run alone.
4. `npm test` green; existing `tests/bin-lib/verify/*` cases pass with only additive assertions.

## Technical Approach

Restore the old rule's universality without losing #1925's precision: keep named-file isolation as the cheap first path and add the whole-suite re-run only where no file can be named. Read the runner's existing `retryDecision` rather than adding new detection, so the prose and the report agree on which path is in force. Do not add a runner-owned whole-suite retry: a full-suite re-run is minutes of work the agent should choose consciously, per the section's own cost note.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/test/verification.md` — Flake handling: two named paths; pre-existing-failures cross-reference
- `plugin/bin/verify.js` — stdout summary clause for a `no-parse` retry decision
- `tests/bin-lib/verify/cli.test.js`, a prose-pin sibling of `tests/verify-scope-declaration.test.js` — new cases

## Gotchas

- The re-run must not write a pass stamp by itself (`stamp.js`'s dirty-tree rule and #1921's stamp semantics stay authoritative); the adjudication is the agent's, the stamp is the runner's.
- `looksPassing` and `extractFailingFiles` are separate: a `no-parse` decision can coexist with a clearly failing exit code, which is exactly the case this record covers. The retry path already strips ANSI before extracting (`verify.js`), so colour alone does not produce `no-parse`; an unknown runner format does.
- `#1837` (shaped in this sweep) adds a vitest dialect and ANSI stripping; once it lands, fewer failures are `no-parse`, but the path still exists for unknown runners.
- Keep the one-re-run cap in prose and in the pin; an unbounded re-run loop is the failure this rule exists to prevent.

## Original request

## Current State
`plugin/skills/test/verification.md` line 151's mandatory isolate-and-rerun-once rule is scoped only to a failure `extractFailingFiles` can name a file for (an "unlisted file" case). A `no-parse` failure (`sniffFamily` returns `generic`, or the extractor can't match the runner's output format) has no isolation procedure at all — it's reported as a flat regression with no flake adjudication, unlike the old universal rule that applied regardless of whether a file could be named.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Extend `verification.md`'s isolate-and-rerun-once procedure to cover the `no-parse` case — e.g. re-running the full suite once (since no single file can be named) before treating a failure as a confirmed regression.
- [ ] Document the distinction between "named-file isolation" and "whole-suite re-run" as the two isolation paths, so a reader can tell which applies.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `verification.md`'s isolation rule explicitly covers both the named-file and no-parse cases.
2. No change to the named-file path's existing behavior.

## Original request
Found by the pre-v6.119.0 whole-branch review (range e7d6d9331..4db32e020): the isolate-and-rerun-once rule regressed from unconditional to named-file-only when #1925's extractor-driven isolation replaced the old universal recipe.

Defer-reason: tangential

groups.title: bin/verify.js: vitest counts parse as null on colour-coded output, so the suite-count regression caveat never fires
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`bin/verify.js` classifies each check's output with `sniffFamily` (`plugin/bin/lib/verify/extract.js`) and parses counts with `parseCounts(text, family)`. Two facts make vitest output unparseable today, and only one of them is the ANSI colour the report names:

1. **The counts path never strips ANSI.** `stripAnsi` exists in `extract.js` (added for #1925's `extractFailingFiles`, whose comment cites this record as the lesson) but is applied only inside `extractFailingFiles`; `sniffFamily`, `parseCounts`, `summaryLine`, and `extractFailingRegion` run on the raw text. A coloured ` FAIL ` or `Tests` line is invisible to the `^FAIL `/`^Tests:` anchors.
2. **Vitest's summary shape is not a recognized family.** `SUMMARY_MARKERS` are jest (`^Tests:.*failed`, `^PASS `/`^FAIL `) and pytest (`^=+ .*(passed|failed).*=+$`); `parseCounts`'s `summary` branch reads only `^Tests:.*$` (colon) or the pytest banner. Vitest prints `Test Files  64 passed (64)` and `Tests  727 passed (727)` — no colon, a `(total)` suffix — so even colour-free vitest output sniffs as `generic` and returns `counts: null`.

`counts: null` is then silent by design at every layer: `report.js` omits the `counts` key (pinned by "counts is omitted from the entry when null"), `verify.js` sets `testCountRegression = null` when `counts.tests` is not a number, and the stdout render prints the CAVEAT line only when a regression object exists. `test/verification.md`'s "Suite-count regression caveat (#881)" section describes the comparison without naming the unparsed case. Neither `run.js` nor `verify.js` sets `NO_COLOR`/`FORCE_COLOR` on the child.

Observed on plugin 6.114.1 (Windows host, pnpm + Vitest 2.x, colour on without a TTY): `counts: null` on both a 64-file and a 43-file suite across two runs, `testCountRegression: null`, while `tests.log` carried both vitest summary lines under escape codes.

Tests: `tests/bin-lib/verify/extract.test.js` (jest and pytest count fixtures; an ANSI case only for `extractFailingFiles`), `report.test.js`, `count-stamp.test.js`, `cli.test.js`.

## Deliverables

- [ ] **Strip ANSI once, before every parser.** In `verify.js`'s check-result composition (the block that calls `sniffFamily`/`summaryLine`/`extractFailingRegion`/`parseCounts`), pass `stripAnsi(text)` to all four; export `stripAnsi` from `extract.js` if it is not already. `extractFailingFiles` keeps its own call (idempotent). The raw log file stays raw.
- [ ] **Recognize vitest.** Add a vitest marker to `SUMMARY_MARKERS` (`^\s*Test Files\s+\d+ (?:passed|failed)` or `^\s*Tests\s+\d+ (?:passed|failed)`) and a vitest branch in `parseCounts`'s `summary` family that reads the `Tests` line: `(\d+) passed`, `(\d+) failed`, `(\d+) skipped`, and the `\((\d+)\)` total, using the same known-category guard as the jest path (an unknown `(\d+) word` phrase blocks derivation rather than guessing). `Test Files` is never used for `counts.tests`; the `Tests` line is.
- [ ] **Belt and braces on colour.** `run.js` spawns the child with `NO_COLOR=1` and `FORCE_COLOR=0` merged into `process.env` (caller values win if already set), so well-behaved runners emit plain text; stripping stays authoritative for runners that ignore both.
- [ ] **Never disable the comparison silently.** When a `tests` check ran, a count stamp is in play, and `counts` parsed `null`, the report entry gains `countsUnparsed: { family }` and the stdout render prints one line in the CAVEAT shape: `CAVEAT: tests counts unparsed (family {family}) — count-stamp comparison skipped; see {logPath}`. `report.testCountRegression` stays `null`. `test/verification.md`'s "Suite-count regression caveat" section gains one sentence naming this line.
- [ ] **Tests.** `extract.test.js`: vitest fixture (coloured and plain) sniffs `summary` and parses `{tests: 727, pass: 727, fail: 0}`; a vitest line with `| 3 failed` parses `fail: 3`; a jest fixture wrapped in ANSI still parses. `report.test.js`: `countsUnparsed` present when set, omitted otherwise. `cli.test.js`: stdout carries the new CAVEAT line for an unparseable `tests` check under `--count-stamp`, and not when counts parse. `run.test.js`: child env carries `NO_COLOR=1`/`FORCE_COLOR=0` without overriding caller-set values.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `parseCounts(stripAnsi(VITEST_COLOURED), sniffFamily(stripAnsi(VITEST_COLOURED)))` returns `{tests: 727, pass: 727, fail: 0}` for the reported output shape; the plain-text equivalent returns the same.
2. Existing jest, pytest, and TAP count fixtures return byte-identical results; the "never a guess" null cases stay null.
3. `node bin/verify.js --count-stamp {p} --cmd tests="{vitest cmd}"` run twice records `checks.tests.counts.tests` both times and prints the drop CAVEAT when the second run's count is lower (fixture-driven in `cli.test.js`).
4. An unparseable `tests` check under a count stamp prints the `CAVEAT: tests counts unparsed` line and sets `countsUnparsed` in `report.json`; no line appears when counts parse or when no stamp is in play.
5. The child process env includes `NO_COLOR=1` and `FORCE_COLOR=0` unless the caller set either.
6. `npm test` green; every existing case in `tests/bin-lib/verify/*` passes unchanged.

## Technical Approach

Strip at the boundary, once, so no parser needs to know about colour; add the vitest shape as a third summary dialect beside jest and pytest rather than loosening the jest regex (a colon-less `Tests` line must not be confused with a TAP `# tests` block — TAP precedence in `sniffFamily` is pinned). Keep counts fail-toward-absence (#892's rule): the new caveat line makes absence visible; it never fabricates a number.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/extract.js` — vitest marker + `parseCounts` branch; export `stripAnsi`
- `plugin/bin/verify.js` — strip before the four parsers; `countsUnparsed`; render the caveat line
- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/run.js` — child env `NO_COLOR`/`FORCE_COLOR`
- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/report.js` — carry `countsUnparsed` into the entry
- `plugin/skills/test/verification.md` — one sentence under "Suite-count regression caveat (#881)"
- `tests/bin-lib/verify/extract.test.js`, `report.test.js`, `cli.test.js`, `run.test.js` — new cases

## Gotchas

- `ANSI_RE` is ESC-anchored on purpose (a literal `[1m` in test output is not a code); keep it, do not widen to bare bracket sequences.
- Vitest prints `Tests` once but `Test Files` too; only the `Tests` line feeds `counts.tests`, or a 64-file suite would be recorded as 64 tests and the drop detector would fire on the wrong axis.
- `count-stamp.js`'s regression compares `previous.tests` to `current.tests` only; the vitest branch must fill `tests` from the parenthesized total when present, else `pass + fail`, matching the jest path's convention.
- Some CI images honour `FORCE_COLOR=1` from the runner's own config over `NO_COLOR`; that is why stripping, not the env, is the fix the acceptance criteria test.

## Original request

**Summary:** `bin/verify.js` records `counts: null` for a `tests` check whose output is vitest's default colour-coded summary (`Tests  64 passed (64)` wrapped in ANSI escape sequences), which silently disables the `--count-stamp` regression comparison the runner documents.

**Kind:** Defect

**Affected component:** `bin/verify.js` (the `tests` summary parser; `_shared`/`test/verification.md`'s "Suite-count regression caveat")

**Repro steps:**
1. In a project whose test command is Vitest (^2.x) with default reporter and colour on (a normal TTY-less `pnpm test` still emits ANSI colour codes on this Windows host), run `node bin/verify.js --count-stamp <path> --cmd tests="pnpm --filter <pkg> test"` twice.
2. Read `report.json` after each run.

**Expected vs. actual:**
Expected: `checks.tests.counts.tests` holds the parsed total (64 test files / N tests here), and the second run compares it against the stamp so a drop would print the documented `CAVEAT:` line.
Actual: `checks.tests.counts` is `null` on both runs (observed twice in one session, on both a core suite of 64 files and a web suite of 43 files), `testCountRegression` is `null`, and no caveat could ever fire — while the raw `tests.log` plainly contains `Test Files  64 passed (64)` / `Tests  727 passed (727)` once ANSI sequences are stripped. The parser appears to match the summary line only when it is free of escape codes.

Suggested fix: strip `\x1b\[[0-9;]*m` before applying the summary regexes (or run the child with `NO_COLOR=1`/`FORCE_COLOR=0` in its env), and surface `counts: null` on a `tests` check as its own visible line rather than silently disabling the comparison.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.114.1

groups.title: test/qa: stories that embed an absolute origin are not rewritten to the resolved APP_URL, so a worktree QA run targets the main checkout's server
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`_shared/dev-url-detection.md` resolves (or starts) a per-worktree dev server and sets
`APP_URL = http://localhost:{port}` (an ephemeral, worktree-isolated port — see its Step 2.7
Worktree Awareness gate). `skills/test/qa-prompts.md`'s Phase 3 dispatch template fills
`{story.url}` verbatim into each dispatched qa-agent's prompt (lines ~76 and ~139: `**URL:**
{story.url}`) — there is no rewrite step anywhere between resolving `APP_URL` and composing that
prompt. A story file that pins an absolute origin (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/...`) therefore
drives whatever server is actually listening on that literal port — the main checkout's server on
the live database — even when `dev-url-detection.md` correctly resolved a different, isolated
`APP_URL` for this worktree run. This is exactly the wrong-code/wrong-data failure Step 2.7's
worktree-awareness gate exists to prevent, except it happens one layer downstream, after
`APP_URL` has already been correctly resolved.

Confirmed on a real run (plugin 6.118.0): four story files pinned absolute origins, two used
root-relative paths; every dispatched qa-agent for the four absolute-origin stories would have
navigated to the wrong server. The operator manually rewrote the origin in every dispatched
prompt by hand (~20 minutes of pre-flight) because the plugin has no documented convention for
whether story `url:` values should be absolute or `APP_URL`-relative, and no rewrite mechanism
either way.

## Deliverables

- At dispatch (`qa-prompts.md`'s Phase 3 template construction, wherever `{story.url}` is
  currently substituted verbatim), when a story's `url` carries an absolute origin
  (scheme+host+port) that differs from the resolved `APP_URL`'s origin, substitute `APP_URL`'s
  origin for the story's own origin, preserving the story's path/query/fragment unchanged.
- Log the rewrite once per run (not once per story) when at least one story needed it — naming
  the original and resolved origins — so a QA report makes clear the substitution happened.
- Document in `stories/SKILL.md` that a story's `url:` field should be a root-relative path
  joined to the resolved `APP_URL` at dispatch time — the convention this record's fix
  establishes — and that an absolute origin, if present, gets its origin rewritten to `APP_URL`'s
  rather than followed literally.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A story with `url: http://127.0.0.1:9999/dashboard` dispatched under a resolved
  `APP_URL = http://localhost:54321` navigates to `http://localhost:54321/dashboard`, not the
  literal `9999` port.
- A story with a root-relative `url: /dashboard` is joined to `APP_URL` unchanged (no regression
  to the already-working case the record's own use case confirms works today).
- The rewrite is logged exactly once per QA run when triggered, not once per affected story.
- `stories/SKILL.md` documents the `url:` field convention (root-relative preferred; an absolute
  origin gets rewritten, not followed literally) where the story schema is otherwise documented.

## Technical Approach

Add the rewrite as a small pure function (parse the story's `url`, and when it carries a
scheme+host+port that differs from the resolved `APP_URL`'s own scheme+host+port, replace just
the origin, keeping path/query/fragment intact — a root-relative `url` needs no parsing branch at
all, since `new URL(story.url, APP_URL).toString()` already does the right thing for both shapes)
applied once, at the point in `qa-prompts.md`'s Phase 3 (or wherever the per-story dispatch prompt
is actually assembled, likely just before the `{story.url}` substitution at lines ~76/139) where
`APP_URL` is already in scope. Log the rewrite via this test pipeline's existing decision-log
convention if a run directory is active, otherwise to the QA report directly
(`qa-reporting.md`'s existing output conventions).

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/test/qa-prompts.md` — apply the origin rewrite before substituting `{story.url}`
  into the Phase 3 dispatch template (~lines 76, 139)
- `plugin/skills/stories/SKILL.md` — document the `url:` field convention
- `plugin/skills/_shared/dev-url-detection.md` — read-only reference: this is where `APP_URL` is
  resolved; not modified by this record

## Gotchas

- Do not silently swallow a story whose origin points at a genuinely different host on purpose
  (e.g. a story deliberately testing an external service, not the app under test) — the rewrite
  should only ever touch the origin, and if a project genuinely needs a story to hit a different
  host, that's outside this record's scope; flag it as a known limitation rather than trying to
  distinguish intent here.
- The log-once-per-run rule (not per-story) matters for QA report readability on a large story
  suite — don't regress it to log every rewritten story individually.

## Original request

**Summary:** `_shared/dev-url-detection.md` resolves (or starts) a per-worktree dev server on a free port, but `qa-procedures.md`'s dispatch passes each story's `url:` verbatim; a story written as `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/...` therefore drives the main checkout's server (wrong code, live database) even when `APP_URL` resolved to the ephemeral worktree port.
**Kind:** Gap
**Affected component:** `skills/test/qa-procedures.md` / `skills/test/qa-prompts.md` / `skills/_shared/dev-url-detection.md`
**Use case:**
Pipeline QA inside a `/claude-tweaks:flow` worktree run (plugin 6.118.0) on a private project whose story files pin absolute origins (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/...` in four files, root-relative paths in two). `dev-url-detection.md` correctly started a dev server on an ephemeral port against a per-worktree test database. Following the procedure literally, every dispatched qa-agent would have navigated to the pinned port — the main checkout's server on the live database — which is exactly the wrong-code/wrong-data case the worktree-awareness step (2.7) warns about. The operator had to rewrite the origin in every dispatched prompt by hand (about 20 minutes of pre-flight before the first story could run), and the plugin offers no place to state the project's convention (absolute story URLs rewritten at dispatch vs. relative paths joined to `APP_URL`).
**Definition:** Clear — at dispatch, substitute the resolved `APP_URL` origin for a story's embedded absolute origin (scheme+host+port) when they differ, log the rewrite once per run, and document in `stories/SKILL.md` that story `url:` values should be root-relative paths joined to `APP_URL`.
**Plugin version:** 6.118.0

groups.title: claim-targets.js: eventually-consistent read-back race + unverified-claim leak
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

Found during a pre-release whole-branch review of `plugin/bin/lib/claim-targets/claim-targets.js`
— all three confirmed still true at this shaping pass:

- **Read-back race** (~line 400): post-write verification (#2073) re-reads immediately with no
  retry/backoff (`if (!verifyClaimLanded(deps, repoSlug, issue, opts.runId, knownTip))`). On the
  contents-API transport `knownTip` is `null`, so the read-back hits GitHub's
  eventually-consistent contents API and can legitimately return the pre-write blob — a spurious
  exit 5 on a claim that actually landed. The file's own header already warns against
  eventually-consistent GitHub reads elsewhere.
- **Claim leak on abort** (~line 227, confirmed): `abort()` releases only `claimedThisRun`
  (`releaseClaimedThisRun(deps, repoSlug, opts.runId, claimedThisRun)`). `stopOrSkip(issue,
  'unverified', 'unverified', 5, {})` runs (confirmed, ~line 401) *before* the target is pushed
  onto `claimedThisRun` (the `claimedThisRun.push(issue)` call is one line after the verification
  check), so a target whose claim genuinely landed (just couldn't be verified back) leaks until
  TTL expiry with no `bot:in-progress` marker making it visible.
- **Stale doc comment** (~line 225, confirmed): `abort()`'s comment still enumerates only exit
  codes 3 and 4 ("`exitCode` is 3 for a `contested`/`inFlight` envelope, 4 for a `transient`
  one") — exit 5 (`unverified`) was added without updating it.

## Deliverables

- Add a bounded retry/backoff to the post-write read-back verification when `knownTip` is `null`,
  before declaring exit 5.
- Release (or otherwise make visible) the `unverified` target's claim on abort, not just
  `claimedThisRun`.
- Update `abort()`'s doc comment to include exit 5.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A simulated eventually-consistent stale read on the contents-API path no longer produces a
  spurious exit 5 within the retry window.
- An aborted run with an `unverified` target leaves that claim in a state a later run can
  detect/reclaim before TTL, not silently leaked.
- `abort()`'s doc comment lists exit codes 3, 4, and 5.
- `npm test` passes.

## Technical Approach

For the read-back race: wrap the `verifyClaimLanded` call (~line 400) in a small bounded
retry loop (a few attempts with a short backoff) specifically for the `knownTip === null` case —
the git-CAS path (`knownTip` set) already has a real tip to compare against and doesn't need
this, since a git-CAS success is immediately consistent. Only declare exit 5 after the retry
window is exhausted. For the claim leak: capture the `unverified` issue's claim state (the
context `verifyClaimLanded` already had before failing) and pass it to `abort()` so it can be
released or explicitly flagged alongside `claimedThisRun`'s own release — the goal is that a
genuinely-landed-but-unverified claim doesn't sit invisible until TTL; releasing it (so a later
run can pick it up cleanly) is the safer default over leaving it silently held. Update the
`abort()` doc comment in the same change.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/claim-targets/claim-targets.js` — the read-back retry (~line 400), the claim
  leak fix (~line 227, `abort()` and the `unverified` stop path), and the doc comment update

## Gotchas

- The retry must be scoped to the `knownTip === null` (contents-API) path only — the git-CAS
  path's `knownTip`-based verification is already immediately consistent and doesn't need
  (or benefit from) a retry; adding one there would just slow down every claim for no
  correctness gain.
- Releasing an `unverified` claim on abort must not race with the claim that write actually
  produced — verify the release targets the same claim identity (`repoSlug`, `issue`, `opts.runId`)
  the write itself used, so a genuinely different run's claim on the same issue is never touched.

## Original request

## Current State
Found during a pre-release whole-branch review of `plugin/bin/lib/claim-targets/claim-targets.js`:

- **Read-back race** (~line 400): post-write verification (#2073) re-reads immediately with no retry/backoff. On the contents-API transport `knownTip` is `null`, so the read-back hits GitHub's eventually-consistent contents API and can legitimately return the pre-write blob — a spurious exit 5 on a claim that actually landed. The file's own header already warns against eventually-consistent GitHub reads elsewhere.
- **Claim leak on abort** (~line 227): `abort()` releases only `claimedThisRun`. `stopOrSkip(issue, 'unverified', 'unverified', 5, {})` runs *before* the target is pushed onto `claimedThisRun` (line ~405), so a target whose claim genuinely landed (just couldn't be verified back) leaks until TTL expiry with no `bot:in-progress` marker making it visible.
- **Stale doc comment** (~line 225): `abort()`'s comment still enumerates only exit codes 3 and 4; exit 5 (`unverified`) was added without updating it.

# Backlog proposal — `--release-as` on the local engine (#2256, ledger row 90)

**Category:** backlog-proposal
**Severity:** low
**Reversibility:** high
**Source:** `/release` Step 5 gap surfaced at #2256's plan phase; `/wrap-up` Phase 3 SETTLE
**Defer-reason:** genuinely-larger
**Proposed title:** Add `--release-as <version>` to `bin/release-local.js` so `/claude-tweaks:release --as` works under local-merge

`/claude-tweaks:release --as <version>` is pr-first only: it pushes a `Release-As:` commit that release-please re-renders. groups.title: Resolve the curation-engine.md dispatch contract vs. project-skill git-mutation conflict
groups.body:
Surface: backend

Origin: ledger resolve gate

Defer-reason: genuinely-larger

## Current State

During record #1276's wrap-up Phase 2 (ROUTE), the Skills-row curation judge followed `.claude/skills/skill-prose-conformance-tests/SKILL.md`'s own "Record the audit" step, which invokes `harness-health.js validate-findings`. That step pushed a commit (`dad090519`) to the remote `health-state` tracking branch — a git mutation. The judge's dispatch prompt, composed per `plugin/skills/wrap-up/curation-engine.md` section 4, explicitly forbids any git mutation ("never run git add, git commit, or any other git mutation"), on the grounds that the controller alone commits, serially, after auditing each finding. The judge grepped the dispatcher for `git`/`spawnSync` beforehand and found nothing — the durable-state write lives on a path that grep missed (inside `harness-health.js`'s own audit-recording mechanism, invoked as a documented step of the project skill it was applying, not as a git command the judge composed itself).

Blast radius was contained: the push landed only on `health-state` (2 files, cursor/run bookkeeping — never the feature branch, never `main`), recorded zero findings, and left the worktree HEAD and working tree exactly as the judge's own edits left them. But the underlying gap is real: `curation-engine.md`'s dispatch contract has no carve-out for a project skill's own legitimate, sanctioned bookkeeping writes to a dedicated tracking branch, so a judge following a project skill's documented procedure can violate the contract without realizing it — the contract and the project skill disagree, and nothing in either file resolves the disagreement.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Decide the resolution direction: either (a) `curation-engine.md`'s dispatch-prompt git-mutation prohibition gets an explicit carve-out for a project skill's own sanctioned bookkeeping branch writes (name the pattern — a push to a branch distinct from the worktree's own feature branch and from the integration branch, or an explicit allowlist), or (b) `.claude/skills/skill-prose-conformance-tests/SKILL.md`'s "Record the audit" step gains a precondition that skips the write when invoked from a context whose contract forbids git mutation (e.g. a documented env var or a passed flag the dispatch prompt sets).
- [ ] Implement the chosen direction.
- [ ] Add a conformance test or explicit inline note documenting the resolved contract, so a future dispatch-contract change doesn't silently reintroduce the conflict.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A Skills-row (or any other curation-engine.md fan-out/singleton) judge dispatch, run against a project whose applicable skill file includes a git-mutating audit-recording step, either completes the write safely under a stated, narrow exception, or the write is skipped with the skip logged — never an unnoticed, unauthorized push.
2. `npm test` passes.

_Filed by `ledger resolve gate`. Close to resolve; label `wontfix` to suppress future reports of this finding._

groups.title: bin/wrap-up-engine.js: render fails silently when the plan/record sequence was skipped
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`wrap-up-engine.js render --section console` fails with no diagnostic output when the run's `record` step was never invoked after `plan` — a caller who performs per-row judgment out-of-band (e.g. via separate `stage-item.js`/`log-decision.js` calls instead of feeding a structured payload back into the engine) gets no indication of what precondition is missing. Observed twice in one session: `--strict` exits 2 with completely empty stdout/stderr; without `--strict` it exits 0 with empty output. Either way there is no actionable signal, and the caller has to infer from source reading that a `record` call was expected and never made — cost roughly 10 extra tool calls reading procedure files and hand-composing the Review Console content instead of one working render call.

## Deliverables

- `render --section console` detects a missing/empty engine-state (no prior `record` call for this run-dir) and fails loud with a specific, actionable message — e.g. "no engine-state.json found for this run-dir — run `record` first."
- This applies under both `--strict` and non-strict invocation: neither mode should produce silent empty output.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Running `render --section console --strict` against a run-dir with a `plan` output but no `record` call exits non-zero with a non-empty, actionable error message naming the missing precondition.
- Running the same command without `--strict` also produces the actionable message (not silent exit 0 with empty output).
- Running `render --section console` against a run-dir that DID complete `record` is unaffected — this fix only changes the missing-precondition path.

## Technical Approach

Locate `render`'s entry point in `plugin/bin/wrap-up-engine.js` (the `--section console` handler) and its read of the run-dir's engine-state file. Add a precondition check before rendering: if the expected engine-state artifact (written by the `record` step) is absent or empty, exit with a clear error naming the missing precondition and the remedy (`run record first`), on both `--strict` and non-strict paths — today the two paths differ only in exit code, both leaving stdout/stderr empty, so the fix should apply the same message to both rather than only fixing one.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/wrap-up-engine.js` — `render --section console` handler and its engine-state read

## Gotchas

- Don't conflate "missing engine-state" with "engine-state present but empty" — both need actionable messages, but a caller reading the error should be able to tell whether `record` was never run at all versus ran but produced nothing.
- Keep the fix scoped to detecting and reporting the missing precondition — do not add a fallback that silently synthesizes a Review Console from a `plan`-only run-dir, which would mask the same problem this fix exists to surface.

## Original request

bin/wrap-up-engine.js: render fails silently when the plan/record sequence was skipped

**Summary:** `wrap-up-engine.js render --section console` fails with no diagnostic output at all when the run's `record` step was never invoked after `plan` — a caller who performs the per-row judgment out-of-band (e.g. via separate `stage-item.js`/`log-decision.js` calls instead of feeding a structured payload back into the engine) gets no indication of what precondition is missing.

**Kind:** Defect

**Affected component:** `bin/wrap-up-engine.js` (`render --section console`)

**Objective:** Friction

**Measurement:** 2 failed render attempts this session (one `--strict` exit 2 with no output, one non-strict exit 0 with empty output) before abandoning the deterministic path for a hand-composed one.

**Cost this session:** roughly 10 extra tool calls reading procedure files and improvising the Review Console's content by hand instead of one working render call.

**Repro steps:**
1. Run `wrap-up-engine.js plan --run-dir <dir> --base <sha> --ceremony standard` — produces a registry plan JSON with several rows (Skills, Docs, Journeys, CLAUDE.md & rules, Decision records, Broken references, Memory, Upstream feedback).
2. Skip the `record` step entirely — perform the judgment for each open-gated row directly (e.g. staging a finding via `stage-item.js` and logging the decision via `log-decision.js`) rather than composing a structured payload and piping it into `wrap-up-engine.js record --run-dir <dir>`.
3. Run `wrap-up-engine.js render --run-dir <dir> --section console --strict`.

**Expected vs. actual:**
Expected: a clear, actionable error naming the missing precondition — e.g. "no engine-state.json found for this run-dir — run `record` first."
Actual: with `--strict`, the command exits 2 with completely empty stdout/stderr. Without `--strict`, it exits 0 with empty output. Either way, there is no information about what is wrong or what to do about it — the caller has to infer from source reading that a `record` call was expected and never made.

**Proposed fix:** `render` should detect a missing/empty engine-state (no prior `record` call) and fail loud with a specific, actionable message, rather than a bare non-zero exit or silent empty output.

**Definition:** Clear.

groups.title: upstream-drift checkOneFixture cannot assert plain-text stderr, only JSON
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`checkOneFixture` in `tools/upstream-drift/checks.js` (lines 330-380) replays a manifest fixture command and asserts its observed output against `expect`. The function hard-requires the named stream (`expect.stream`, `stdout` or `stderr`) to parse as JSON — `tryParseJson(streams[wanted].trim())` — and returns a mismatch if it doesn't, including a special case that names when the JSON payload landed on the other stream instead. This makes it impossible to write a fixture for a command whose failure output is plain text rather than JSON. This was discovered while auditing #2480 (Impeccable CLI Rust-engine shim): the engine-locate/download failure path writes a plain-text message to stderr and exits 127, but there is no way to assert that exact behavior as a fixture today — only a JSON-shaped stderr/stdout payload is expressible.

## Deliverables
1. Extend `checkOneFixture` to support a plain-text/substring assertion mode on a named stream, as an alternative to the existing JSON-parse assertion — expressible via a new `expect` field (e.g. `expect.contains` or `expect.textMatch`) that, when present, asserts a substring match on `streams[expect.stream]` instead of requiring JSON parse.
2. Update the manifest schema/validation (`tools/upstream-drift/manifest.js`) to accept the new field alongside the existing `exit`/`stream`/`keys` fields, validating that a fixture specifies either the JSON-mode fields or the new text-mode field, not an ambiguous mix.
3. Add a fixture to `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml` (or a test-only manifest) exercising the plain-text stderr case from #2480 (or an equivalent), to prove the new mode round-trips a real plain-text failure.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. A fixture whose `expect` includes the new text-mode field and a substring that appears in the named stream's actual output passes `checkOneFixture`.
2. A fixture whose `expect` includes the new text-mode field and a substring that does NOT appear in the named stream's actual output returns a `mismatch` result with a detail naming the expected substring and which stream was checked.
3. Existing JSON-mode fixtures (using `expect.keys`) are unaffected — `checkOneFixture`'s existing JSON-parse path and its stdout/stderr swap detection continue to work exactly as before for fixtures that don't use the new field.
4. The manifest validation in `manifest.js` accepts fixtures using the new text-mode field without requiring the JSON-mode `keys` field, and still validates `exit`/`stream` are present as it does today.
5. A fixture reproducing the #2480 plain-text-stderr/exit-127 case round-trips correctly (passes when the actual behavior matches, fails with an informative detail when it regresses).

## Technical Approach
Add a new optional `expect` field for text/substring assertion, checked in `checkOneFixture` before or alongside the existing JSON-parse branch: if the text-mode field is present, skip the JSON-parse requirement entirely and instead check `streams[wanted].includes(expectedSubstring)`, returning a `mismatch` with a clear detail (naming the expected substring and observed stream) on failure. Keep the existing JSON-parse path unchanged for fixtures that don't opt into the new field — the two modes should be mutually exclusive per fixture, decided by which `expect` fields are present. Update `manifest.js`'s fixture validation to allow this new field and to require that a fixture uses exactly one assertion mode (JSON-mode via `keys`, or text-mode via the new field) rather than allowing both or neither silently.

### Key Files
- `tools/upstream-drift/checks.js` — `checkOneFixture` (lines 330-380): add the text/substring assertion branch, keep the JSON-parse path unchanged for non-opted-in fixtures
- `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.js` — fixture schema validation: accept the new `expect` field, enforce mutually-exclusive assertion mode
- `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml` — add or extend a fixture exercising the plain-text-stderr case from #2480
- `tools/upstream-drift/tests/manifest.test.js` — add test coverage for the new field's validation
- `tools/upstream-drift/tests/checks.test.js` (if it exists; otherwise the relevant checks test file) — add test coverage for the new text-mode assertion branch in `checkOneFixture`

## Gotchas
The two assertion modes (JSON-parse vs. text/substring) must stay mutually exclusive per fixture — allowing both to be specified together would create ambiguous validation semantics. The existing stdout/stderr-swap detection in the JSON-parse path is a load-bearing anti-regression check (comment at checks.js:361-366 calls it "the single most important case this function exists to catch"); the new text-mode path does not need to replicate that specific swap-detection logic unless a plain-text payload swap becomes a realized failure mode worth catching, but should not regress the existing JSON-mode swap detection.

## Original request

upstream-drift checkOneFixture cannot assert plain-text stderr, only JSON

**Related:** #2480

Context: Discovered auditing #2480 (Impeccable CLI Rust-engine shim) -- the engine-locate/download failure writes a plain-text message to stderr and exits 127, but checkOneFixture (tools/upstream-drift/checks.js:359-369) hard-requires the asserted stream to parse as JSON.

Scope: Extend checkOneFixture (or add a sibling assertion mode) to support a text/substring match on a named stream, so a plain-text failure like this becomes expressible as a fixture.

groups.title: wrap-up verify: carrier-commit check only matches the literal "Fixes #N", missing GitHub's other closing keywords
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.js`'s `carrier-commit` check (`registerCheck('carrier-commit', …)`, line ~320) verifies that each resolved issue in a wrap-up run has a "carrier commit" that closed it. The check currently greps the branch log for the literal string `Fixes #{n}` only (line ~330: `deps.git(['log', '--grep=Fixes #${n}', ...])`), and, when a PR-first fallback is needed, checks the PR body for the same literal string (line ~345: `prBody.includes('Fixes #${n}')`).

GitHub recognizes a broader set of closing keywords in commit messages and PR bodies — `close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved` (case-insensitive, optionally `owner/repo#N`) — any of which actually closes the linked issue on merge. Because this check only recognizes the literal `Fixes #N` form, a run whose commits used any other recognized keyword (e.g. `Closes #N`) fails the check with `missing` populated for every record, even though GitHub's own state shows the issues correctly closed. This was observed on a real four-record standalone wrap-up (commits used `Closes #N`; all four issues were CLOSED at merge time; `verify` still exited 3 and `execution-and-verification.md`'s exit-3 → BLOCKED rule fired incorrectly), on plugin 6.127.0.

The repo already has a reusable mechanism for checking an issue's actual closing state via GraphQL: `plugin/bin/lib/issues/linked-prs.js`'s `fetchLinkedPRs` resolves each candidate issue's `closedByPullRequestsReferences` connection in one batched call — this is the "ground truth" data source the bug report's proposed fix references.

A related, separately-tracked false-negative in the same verify table is #2552 (`run-dir-archived`) — not in scope here, but worth being aware the verify table has more than one known false-negative row.

## Deliverables
1. Replace the `carrier-commit` check's branch-log grep (line ~330) with a case-insensitive match over GitHub's full recognized closing-keyword set (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`), each optionally preceded by `owner/repo` before the `#N`, matching against `#{n}` as a whole reference (not a substring of a larger number).
2. Apply the same keyword-set widening to the PR-body fallback check (line ~345), which currently has the identical literal-`Fixes` narrowing.
3. Add a ground-truth fallback: when neither the branch-log grep nor the PR-body check finds a carrier commit for an issue, query the issue's actual state via `gh issue view N --json state` (or reuse `plugin/bin/lib/issues/linked-prs.js`'s `fetchLinkedPRs`/`closedByPullRequestsReferences` connection) and treat a CLOSED state backed by a closing PR/commit reference as a pass on its own, rather than failing purely because no commit message matched a keyword pattern.
4. Keep the existing `fail` behavior for a genuinely-open issue with no matching commit and no closing reference — the fix narrows false negatives, it does not weaken the check's ability to catch a real missing carrier commit.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `carrier-commit` passes for a run whose closing commit message uses any of GitHub's recognized closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`), case-insensitive, with or without an `owner/repo#N` prefix — not just the literal `Fixes #N` form.
- The PR-body fallback check recognizes the same keyword set as the branch-log check (no longer just `Fixes #N`).
- `carrier-commit` passes for an issue that is CLOSED with a `closedByPullRequestsReferences`/closing-commit reference, even if no commit message in the branch range matched any keyword pattern textually (the ground-truth fallback).
- `carrier-commit` still fails (`missing` populated) for an issue with no matching commit message, no matching PR body reference, and no closing-PR-reference-backed CLOSED state — a genuinely missing carrier commit is still caught.
- `tests/bin-lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.test.js` gains test cases covering: a `Closes #N` commit (currently would fail, should now pass), a `Resolves #N` commit, case-insensitivity (`FIXES #N`), and the ground-truth CLOSED-state fallback path.
- Existing passing test cases in `tests/bin-lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.test.js` for the `carrier-commit` check (including the literal `Fixes #N` case) continue to pass.

## Technical Approach
Read `plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.js` lines ~306-345 (the `carrier-commit` check and its preceding comment block) and `tests/bin-lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.test.js`'s existing `carrier-commit` test cases before changing anything, to preserve the check's existing pr-first/local-merge branching logic (the comment block above the check, lines ~312-318, explains why the PR-body fallback exists only when `resolvePrNumber` resolves a PR — don't disturb that branching, only the keyword-matching and add the new ground-truth fallback). Build the keyword regex once (a shared constant, since it's needed in three places: the git log `--grep`, the PR body match, and potentially reused by any other check that does closing-keyword matching) rather than inlining it three times. For the ground-truth fallback, reuse `plugin/bin/lib/issues/linked-prs.js`'s existing `fetchLinkedPRs` rather than writing a new GraphQL query — it already resolves `closedByPullRequestsReferences` in one batched call across all candidate issues, matching this check's existing per-issue loop shape.

### Key Files
- `plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.js` — widen the `--grep` pattern (line ~330) and the PR-body check (line ~345) to the full keyword set; add the ground-truth CLOSED-state fallback to `registerCheck('carrier-commit', ...)`
- `plugin/bin/lib/issues/linked-prs.js` — reuse `fetchLinkedPRs` for the ground-truth fallback rather than writing new GraphQL query logic
- `tests/bin-lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.test.js` — add test cases for the widened keyword set, case-insensitivity, and the ground-truth fallback path; verify no regression on the existing `Fixes #N` case

## Gotchas
- Preserve the existing pr-first/local-merge branching logic (the comment at lines ~312-318) — the fix is about widening keyword matching and adding a ground-truth fallback, not restructuring when the PR-body check applies vs. the branch-log check.
- The keyword regex must match `#N` as a whole issue reference, not a substring of a larger number (e.g. `#12` should not match inside `#123`) — use a word boundary or equivalent anchor.
- `owner/repo#N` is a valid GitHub closing-keyword form too (per the bug report) — the regex/match should account for it, not just bare `#N`.
- The ground-truth fallback adds a `gh` (or GraphQL) call — keep it scoped to only the issues that fail the textual match, not run unconditionally for every issue, to avoid unnecessary API calls on the common case where the textual match already succeeds.
- #2552 (`run-dir-archived`) is a separate, already-filed false-negative in the same verify table — do not fold its fix into this record; it has its own scope.

## Original request

wrap-up verify: carrier-commit check only matches the literal "Fixes #N", missing GitHub's other closing keywords

**Summary:** `wrap-up-engine.js verify`'s `carrier-commit` check greps the branch log for the literal `Fixes #N` only, so a run whose closing commits used GitHub's other closing keywords (`Closes #N`, `Resolves #N`, `Fixed #N`, etc.) fails the check even though GitHub closed the issues on merge.

**Kind:** Defect

**Affected component:** `bin/lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.js` (`registerCheck('carrier-commit', …)`), and the `skills/wrap-up/execution-and-verification.md` exit-3 → BLOCKED rule that consumes it

**Repro steps:**
1. On a `local-merge` project, fix a record in a worktree and commit with a footer line `Closes #N` (GitHub's documented closing keyword) instead of `Fixes #N`.
2. Rebase-merge to the integration branch; GitHub closes issue #N.
3. Run `/claude-tweaks:wrap-up #N`; at Phase 4's Verify step, `node bin/wrap-up-engine.js verify --run-dir <run-dir> --base <sha>`.

**Expected vs. actual:**
Expected: `carrier-commit` passes — the range contains a commit whose message closes #N with any keyword GitHub recognizes (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`, case-insensitive, optionally `owner/repo#N`), and the issue is in fact closed.
Actual: `deps.git(['log', '--grep=Fixes #N', …])` finds nothing, `missing` fills with every record, the row reads `fail — no carrier commit found for #N, …`, verify exits 3, and the skill's rule forbids the closure line on a run that closed all its records. Observed on a four-record standalone wrap-up (commits used `Closes #N`; all four issues showed CLOSED at merge time), plugin 6.127.0.

Proposed fix: match with a case-insensitive regex over GitHub's closing-keyword set (`--grep` with `-i -E '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?) #N\b'`, or read the log once and match in JS), and — since the issue's own state is the ground truth — treat a `gh issue view N --json state` of CLOSED with a `closedByPullRequestsReferences`/closing-commit reference as a pass on its own. The PR-body fallback has the same literal-`Fixes` narrowing (`prBody.includes('Fixes #N')`) and should use the same set.

**Related:** #2552 (run-dir-archived, the other false-negative row in the same verify table)

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.127.0

groups.title: Flag polling-vs-realtime and duplicate-version anti-patterns
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
Two recurring coding-agent anti-patterns have been identified from an external source (a transcribed Instagram Reel from a developer who has shipped 15+ AI-built apps):

1. **Polling instead of realtime push** — agents building a data flow that needs live updates default to fixed-interval polling (e.g. `setInterval` fetches every few seconds) instead of a realtime push/subscription mechanism when the backend already supports one (e.g. a Supabase/Convex subscription, a websocket, SSE). This looks fine in testing but drains battery and degrades frame rate under real usage.
2. **Duplicate "v2" files instead of in-place edits** — agents avoid replacing working code in place, instead layering a `v2`/duplicate-suffixed file or function on top "just in case." This leaves dead code around, and the agent loses track of which version is actually live, leading to circular, self-breaking edits on later requests.

Anti-pattern 2 is already a standing instruction in this repo's own CLAUDE.md ("don't use feature flags or backwards-compatibility shims when you can just change the code" — see the Philosophy/Don'ts sections) — the external source is independent confirmation that the same failure mode is common enough across coding agents generally to be worth a dedicated automated review check, not just a written instruction the agent might drift from under pressure.

Neither anti-pattern currently has an automated review-lens check.

## Deliverables
1. Add a review-lens check that flags a newly introduced fixed-interval polling loop (`setInterval`/`setTimeout` recursion, or an equivalent polling construct) against a data source that already exposes or could reasonably expose a realtime push/subscription mechanism.
2. Add a review-lens check that flags a newly created file or function with a version-suffix name pattern (`v2`, `-new`, `-copy`, `_updated`, etc.) sitting alongside an unremoved original that the diff did not delete or fully migrate away from.
3. Document that these two checks formalize the existing CLAUDE.md "change code in place" instruction into an automated check, rather than relying on the instruction alone.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The polling check flags a sample diff that adds a fixed-interval polling loop against a realtime-capable backend.
- The polling check does not flag polling against a data source with no realtime alternative available (e.g. a third-party REST API with no push option).
- The duplicate-version check flags a sample diff that introduces a `v2`-suffixed (or equivalent) file/function alongside its unremoved original.
- The duplicate-version check does not flag a legitimate versioned artifact (e.g. an API route intentionally versioned as `/v2/` for external consumers) — the check targets abandoned/duplicated internal code, not a deliberate external contract.
- Documentation for the review-lens (or the relevant skill's checklist) states that these two checks formalize the existing CLAUDE.md instruction into an automated check.

## Technical Approach
Locate where existing review-lens checks live (likely under `/claude-tweaks:review`'s checks or a related lens-definition file) and read at least one existing check to match its structure and severity/reporting conventions. Add the two new checks following that same structure, including copy-paste-able flag conditions and a false-positive guard for each (realtime-unavailable backends for the polling check; deliberately-versioned external contracts for the duplicate-version check).

### Key Files
- (the review-lens check definitions directory — identify exact path via the `/claude-tweaks:review` skill before editing; not yet confirmed in this record)

## Gotchas
- The exact location of existing review-lens check definitions is not confirmed in this record — locate it first rather than assuming a path.
- The duplicate-version check must not fire on legitimate, deliberately-versioned external-facing artifacts (API routes, published package majors) — only on abandoned/duplicated internal code from indecisive in-place-edit avoidance.
- The polling check must not fire when no realtime alternative exists for the given backend/data source — polling is the correct choice there, not an anti-pattern.

## Original request

Flag polling-vs-realtime and duplicate-version anti-patterns

Current State:
- Reel (hook-only caption; transcribed), from a developer who has shipped 15+ AI-built apps, names two recurring coding-agent anti-patterns: (1) agents default to polling the server every few seconds instead of using a realtime push mechanism (e.g. Supabase/Convex subscriptions), draining battery and degrading frame rate under real usage even though it feels fine in testing; (2) agents avoid replacing code in place, instead layering a "v2" on top of the working version "just in case," which leaves dead code around and causes the agent to lose track of which version is live, leading to circular, self-breaking edits on later requests.
- The second anti-pattern is already addressed as a standing instruction in this session's own CLAUDE.md guidance ("don't use feature flags or backwards-compatibility shims when you can just change the code") — this reel is independent confirmation the same failure mode is common enough to be worth a dedicated automated check, not just a written instruction the agent might drift from.

Deliverables:
- Add a review-lens check for: (a) new realtime data flows implemented as fixed-interval polling instead of push/subscription where the backend supports it; (b) newly created "v2"/duplicate-suffixed files or functions sitting alongside an unremoved original.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Check flags a sample polling loop and a sample duplicate-version file pair.
- Docs note this formalizes an existing CLAUDE.md instruction into an automated check rather than relying on the instruction alone.

groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

The Impeccable/design-review lens has no explicit rules for count badges vs. status dots (when to combine, when they collide). No guidance distinguishes "something changed" (dot) from "how much" (number), or governs badge color semantics (red = act now, green = online). No rule flags a badge that lingers after the user has already viewed the item, or a count that resets to zero instead of ticking down.

## Deliverables

- A policy row (or lens check) for badge/dot usage: one signal per element, color tied to meaning, clears on view.
- A check for "badge everything" anti-patterns that dilute color meaning.
- Reference the source technique inline so the check has a rationale, not just a rule.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Running the design-review lens on a UI with a badge flags a dual dot+counter on the same element.
- The check explains why (noise / trained-to-ignore) rather than just failing silently.

## Technical Approach

Follow this repo's existing design-review lens/policy-row pattern (`design-wrapper`'s Impeccable-routed passes) rather than inventing a new check mechanism. Add the badge/dot rule as a new policy row: flag an element carrying both a status dot and a count badge simultaneously (dual signal), flag a badge color that doesn't map to the established red/green (or equivalent) meaning convention, and flag a badge/count pattern description that never mentions clearing on view. Each flagged violation's message should name the specific rule violated and a one-line rationale (noise / trained-to-ignore), per the Acceptance Criteria.

groups.title: Add a typographic-system checklist to the UI review lens
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

The design-review lens has no check for typographic-system discipline: font count, a fixed type-scale ratio, or a capped weight count. No rule catches hand-picked pixel sizes, uniform line-height across headings/body, or unbounded paragraph measure (characters per line). No check for tabular figures on numeric/price/timer UI, which is what stops columns from wobbling on data updates. Competitive note: a third-party Claude Code plugin ("UX engine") designs the screen before coding and audits diffs for an "AI look" — worth knowing about as adjacent to Impeccable.

## Deliverables

- A policy row for a bounded type scale (one ratio, capped sizes/weights) and capped line length (45-75 characters).
- A check for tabular-nums usage on numeric UI.
- A short note in Impeccable's own docs flagging the competing "UX engine" tool as a reference point.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Running the lens on a UI with unbounded font sizes or an unmeasured paragraph flags it with the specific rule violated.

## Technical Approach

Follow this repo's existing design-review lens/policy-row pattern (`design-wrapper`'s Impeccable-routed passes) rather than inventing a new check mechanism. Add three checks: (1) type-scale discipline — flag font-size values not derived from a single declared ratio, or a font/weight count exceeding a capped threshold; (2) line-length — flag a paragraph measure outside 45-75 characters per line; (3) tabular figures — flag numeric/price/timer UI not using tabular-nums (or equivalent fixed-width digit styling). Each flagged violation names the specific rule violated, per the Acceptance Criteria.

groups.title: Add classic friction-reduction UX laws to the review lens
groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

The design-review lens has no checks tied to the classic conversion/friction heuristics: choice count (Hick's Law), tap-target/CTA affordance (Fitts's Law), navigation familiarity (Jacob's Law), or chunked identifiers like phone numbers and codes (Miller's Law). No check for a journey's peak/end moments (Peak-End Rule), spatial grouping of related controls (Proximity), or a single visually distinct emphasis element (Von Restorff Effect).

## Deliverables

- A policy row per law: too-many-options, small/ambiguous primary actions, unfamiliar nav patterns, unchunked numeric IDs, no memorable peak/end step, ungrouped related controls, no standout CTA.
- Cite the law by name in the check's explanation so violations are self-documenting.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Running the lens on a form with 10+ ungrouped choices or an unchunked ID field flags the specific law violated.

## Technical Approach

Follow this repo's existing design-review lens/policy-row pattern (`design-wrapper`'s Impeccable-routed passes, the same mechanism #2706/#2707 extend) rather than inventing a new check mechanism. Add seven policy rows, one per named heuristic, each citing the law by name in its violation message: choice-count threshold (Hick's), minimum tap-target size (Fitts's), navigation-pattern familiarity (Jacob's), numeric-ID chunking (Miller's), peak/end moment presence in multi-step journeys (Peak-End), spatial grouping of related controls (Proximity), and single-standout-CTA presence (Von Restorff).

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/design-wrapper/modes/` — wherever the design-review lens's policy rows are defined, for the seven new checks

## Gotchas

- This is the third UI-review-lens checklist addition from the same source series (#2706, #2707, #2709) — consider whether all three should land in one consolidated lens-extension pass rather than three separate small PRs, to avoid repeated churn on the same policy-row file.
- Some of these heuristics (Peak-End Rule, Von Restorff Effect) are more subjective/journey-level than the others (tap-target size, ID chunking, which are directly measurable) — keep the check's confidence/certainty language honest per heuristic rather than treating all seven as equally mechanical.

## Original request

Add classic friction-reduction UX laws to the review lens

Current State:
- The design-review lens has no checks tied to the classic conversion/friction heuristics: choice count (Hick's Law), tap-target/CTA affordance (Fitts's Law), navigation familiarity (Jacob's Law), or chunked identifiers like phone numbers and codes (Miller's Law).
- No check for a journey's peak/end moments (Peak-End Rule), spatial grouping of related controls (Proximity), or a single visually distinct emphasis element (Von Restorff Effect).

Deliverables:
- A policy row per law: too-many-options, small/ambiguous primary actions, unfamiliar nav patterns, unchunked numeric IDs, no memorable peak/end step, ungrouped related controls, no standout CTA.
- Cite the law by name in the check's explanation so violations are self-documenting.

Acceptance Criteria:
